title: Parasite life cycles: the long journey from one host to the next

summary.text: In dry parts of India, people once drank from step wells, and about a year later a worm as long as an arm pushed out through the skin of their foot. The worm was never in the water as a worm. She began as a speck inside a tiny water animal that nobody noticed. A folded piece of old sari cloth over the pot stopped her. Your child tests which cloth catches pretend water animals and how fast the water flows through, then follows the journeys of the Guinea worm, the filaria worm, the malaria parasite and a liver fluke, and finds out why a parasite that must pass through several bodies has to lay thousands of eggs so that one of them may succeed.
summary.art: A woman stretching a folded old sari cloth over the mouth of a clay matka and pouring water through it, while a tiny water animal as big as a poppy seed is drawn large in a circle beside her.

intro.hook: Pour a glass of water through a folded cloth. The water looks the same before and after. Yet in India, a folded cloth over a pot helped to stop an illness that had lasted for thousands of years. What was the cloth catching?
intro.text: In this unit you find out what the cloth caught, and why one cloth could end a whole illness. You test cloths of your own with pretend water animals. You follow a parasite from an egg, through a tiny animal, into a person, and out again. You find out why a parasite lays thousands of eggs, and why cutting the journey at one weak link can stop it for good.
intro.art: A glass of clear water on a table, a square of folded cotton cloth beside it with a few tiny specks caught on the surface, and a magnifying glass over the specks.

outcomes: I can describe a life cycle, and say what a final host, an intermediate host and a vector are.
I can follow the journey of the Guinea worm through a person and a tiny water animal, and say two ways that stopped it.
I can explain how a filter holds back things bigger than its gaps, and why a finer filter lets water through more slowly.
I can explain why a parasite lays so many eggs, by multiplying the odds at each stage.
I can describe how a mosquito carries the filaria worm and the malaria parasite, and why malaria fever comes in waves.
I can say how a liver fluke, a tapeworm and a mite each reach a new host, and how to break each journey.
I can choose the weakest link in a life cycle, and say what would break it.
I can tell how Patrick Manson's wrong guess about the filaria worm was shown to be wrong by George Low.

terms.meaning: The series of stages a living being goes through, from an egg to an adult who makes new eggs.
terms.example: A mosquito has four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult.
terms.art: Four pictures in a circle with arrows: a mosquito egg raft, a wriggler, a pupa and an adult mosquito.

terms.meaning: One step in a life cycle. A being at different stages can look and live very differently.
terms.example: A Guinea worm larva is smaller than a grain of sand. The adult female can be as long as an arm.
terms.art: A tiny speck beside a grain of sand, and beside them a long coiled worm laid next to a forearm.

terms.meaning: The young form of an animal that looks very different from the adult.
terms.example: A mosquito larva is a wriggler that hangs from the surface of still water.
terms.art: Several wrigglers hanging head down from the surface of water in a bowl, with a breathing tube touching the surface.

terms.meaning: A tough resting stage with a hard coat, that can survive outside a body for days or weeks.
terms.example: Amoeba and Giardia are single-celled parasites. Their cysts can sit in dirty water until someone drinks it.
terms.art: A round cyst with a thick coat drawn beside a soft amoeba with no coat.

terms.meaning: The host in which a parasite becomes an adult and makes eggs or young.
terms.example: A person is the final host of the Guinea worm.
terms.art: A person with a long worm coiled under the skin of a leg, labelled adult.

terms.meaning: A host in which a parasite grows through a young stage but does not become an adult.
terms.example: A copepod is the intermediate host of the Guinea worm. A snail is the intermediate host of the liver fluke.
terms.art: A copepod with a tiny curled larva inside her, labelled young stage.

terms.meaning: A living being who carries a parasite or a germ from one host to another. The vector is usually not the one who gets ill.
terms.example: The Culex mosquito is the vector of the filaria worm.
terms.art: A mosquito drawn as a small boat carrying a tiny thread-like worm between two sleeping people.

terms.meaning: A tiny water animal, about as big as a poppy seed or a little bigger. Many swim in ponds and wells, and people often call them water fleas.
terms.example: A copepod swims by jerks. A cloth filter can catch copepods.
terms.art: A copepod drawn large from above, pear-shaped with two long feelers and a pair of egg sacs.

terms.meaning: A long thin worm that lives under the skin of a person's leg or foot. Her life cycle needs a person and a copepod.
terms.example: India was certified free of Guinea worm in 2000.
terms.art: A thin white worm coming out of a blister on a foot, wound a little round a matchstick.

terms.meaning: A group of thread-like worms that live in the lymph vessels, the thin tubes that drain fluid from the body. Mosquitoes carry them from person to person.
terms.example: Filaria can cause very swollen legs, which people call elephantiasis.
terms.art: A mosquito biting an arm, and beside the arm a magnified drop of blood with tiny thread-like worms in it.

terms.meaning: A flat, leaf-shaped worm that lives as a parasite. Many flukes use a snail as their first host.
terms.example: The liver fluke lives in the liver of cattle and buffalo.
terms.art: A flat leaf-shaped fluke drawn large, beside a small pond snail.

terms.meaning: A tiny eight-legged animal, related to spiders and ticks, often too small to see. Some mites live in the skin.
terms.example: The scabies mite digs shallow tunnels in the top layer of skin.
terms.art: A round mite with eight short legs drawn very large next to a full stop for scale.

terms.meaning: An itchy skin illness caused by a mite that burrows into the top layer of the skin. It spreads by close skin contact.
terms.example: The itch of scabies is worst at night.
terms.art: A child scratching a wrist with a rash of small red spots between the fingers.

terms.meaning: When an illness comes back after a person felt well. Some malaria parasites sleep in the liver and wake up later.
terms.example: A person treated for vivax malaria can have a relapse months later.
terms.art: A temperature line that falls to normal, stays flat for weeks and then rises again.

terms.meaning: The pattern of gaps in a net, a cloth or a filter. A fine mesh has very small gaps.
terms.example: A mosquito net has a finer mesh than a cricket net.
terms.art: Two squares of cloth magnified: one with wide gaps between threads and one with tiny gaps.

terms.meaning: Something with tiny gaps that lets water pass but holds back bigger things.
terms.example: A tea strainer is a filter. It holds back tea leaves and lets the tea through.
terms.art: A tea strainer over a cup, with tea leaves caught on the mesh and tea falling through.

terms.meaning: When every person in a place at risk is given a medicine on the same days, even if they feel well, to clear a parasite from the whole community.
terms.example: In some districts of India, everyone is offered tablets once a year to clear filaria worms from the blood.
terms.art: A health worker handing tablets and a cup of water to a line of villagers outside a school.

terms.meaning: To eliminate is to stop an illness spreading in one place, such as a country. To eradicate is to stop it everywhere in the world.
terms.example: Smallpox has been eradicated. Guinea worm has been eliminated from India and is close to being eradicated.
terms.art: A map of the world with red dots in a few countries, and next to it a map with no dots.

terms.meaning: A substance put into water to kill mosquito larvae or other young stages.
terms.example: Health workers put a larvicide in ponds and step wells.
terms.art: A health worker pouring a measured packet of larvicide into a pond with wrigglers visible below.

explanations.concept: What a life cycle is, and why a parasite needs several homes
explanations.context: This card says what a life cycle is, and names the different hosts a parasite can use.
explanations.definition: A life cycle is the series of stages a living being passes through. A parasite's cycle often needs more than one kind of host.
explanations.description: A free-living animal, such as a frog, has a life cycle too. Egg, tadpole, frog, egg again. A parasite's cycle is harder, because every stage must find the right body. A final host is the body where the parasite becomes an adult and makes eggs. An intermediate host is a body where a young stage grows but does not become an adult. A vector is a carrier, like a mosquito, who moves a parasite from one host to the next. Not every parasite uses all three. A louse uses one host for the whole life. The Guinea worm uses two, a copepod and a person. The malaria parasite uses two, a person and a mosquito. A liver fluke uses three, a snail, a plant and a cow. Each extra host is one more place where the journey can fail, and one more place where people can cut it.
examples: A head louse lives all of her life on one person, so she has only one host.
The Guinea worm needs a copepod and a person, so she has two hosts.
The liver fluke needs a snail, then grass or a water plant, then a cow or buffalo, so she has three homes.
explanations.art: Three journeys drawn as arrows: one circle for a louse, a line between a copepod and a person for the Guinea worm, and a line through a snail, a plant and a cow for the liver fluke.

explanations.concept: The Guinea worm: a journey through a person and a water animal
explanations.context: This card follows the Guinea worm all the way round. It shows the journey that a folded cloth helped to cut.
explanations.definition: The Guinea worm is a parasitic worm whose life cycle needs a person as the final host and a copepod as the intermediate host.
explanations.description: A person drinks water that holds copepods. Some copepods carry baby worms, which are called larvae. Stomach acid kills the copepods, and frees the larvae. The larvae go through the wall of the gut and grow. About a year later, a female worm, about 70 to 120 centimetres long, moves to the skin of a leg or foot and makes a painful blister. The burning makes the person put the foot into water. The worm pushes out her head and lets out a cloud of tiny larvae. A copepod swallows the larvae. Inside the copepod the larvae grow for about two weeks, until they are ready to infect a person. Nobody can catch the Guinea worm from another person, or from touching the worm. People catch the worm only by drinking the water with the copepods. For centuries the worm was drawn out slowly, a little each day, round a stick. In dry parts of India, such as Rajasthan, people drank from step wells and ponds that were full of copepods. From the 1980s, health workers taught people to filter their water through cloth, and to keep an infected foot out of the water. They also treated ponds and step wells, and later dug wells and laid pipes. India was certified free of Guinea worm in 2000. In the 1980s there were several million cases a year in many countries, and now there are only a handful.
examples: Larvae in a copepod take about two weeks to be ready. A person who drinks the copepod a year before the blister shows has no idea.
A person with a blister who keeps the foot out of the village water breaks the journey at the first link.
A cloth over the pot holds the copepods back, which breaks the journey at the second link.
explanations.art: A circle of five pictures with arrows: a person drinking from a step well, a larva leaving the gut, a long worm under the skin of a foot, a blister touching water, and a copepod swallowing larvae.

explanations.concept: Filters: a size gate, and the price of a finer one
explanations.context: This card explains how a cloth filter works and what it cannot do. You tested this yourself.
explanations.definition: A filter is a barrier with tiny gaps. It lets water and everything smaller than the gaps pass, and holds back everything bigger.
explanations.description: A filter is not a trap. It is a gate with a fixed width. Anything wider than the gaps stays on top, and anything narrower goes through. A copepod is about one to two millimetres long, as big as a poppy seed or a little bigger. A fine cotton cloth has gaps much narrower than that, so it holds the copepods back. But a gate that holds back more things also lets less water through. A cloth folded into four layers has narrower and longer gaps than one layer, so it catches more, and the water passes more slowly. A filter has another limit. Germs are a thousand times smaller than a copepod, and dissolved things are smaller still. A cloth does not catch them. So a cloth stops the Guinea worm's copepods, but does not make water free of bacteria, viruses or chemicals. For those, water must be boiled, treated or passed through a finer filter, such as a ceramic candle. A cloth filter is a good first step. It is not the last one.
examples: A tea strainer holds back leaves but lets the tea through, and the same idea holds back copepods when the gaps are small enough.
Turmeric stirred into water stays yellow after a cloth, because the colour is made of pieces much smaller than the gaps.
A ceramic candle filter has gaps small enough to hold back many bacteria, so it takes much longer to drip.
explanations.art: Three squares of mesh, magnified: wide gaps with a large speck passing, medium gaps with the speck caught, and tiny gaps with a speck caught and a water drop passing slowly.

explanations.concept: Why a parasite lays so many eggs: the odds multiply
explanations.context: This card explains why parasites make huge numbers of eggs, using the odds at each stage of a journey.
explanations.definition: The chance of a parasite finishing her whole journey is the chances at every stage multiplied together.
explanations.description: Suppose an egg has a 1 in 10 chance of getting through each of four stages. Maybe it must land in water, then be eaten by the right animal, then grow, then reach a person. The chance of finishing all four is 1 in 10, then 1 in 100, then 1 in 1,000, then 1 in 10,000. So to get one adult, the parasite needs about ten thousand eggs. Real parasites have worse odds than that, so they make many thousands. A female roundworm can lay many thousands of eggs a day. A tapeworm releases whole segments full of eggs. A liver fluke gets help from a snail, because one young fluke inside a snail makes hundreds of copies of herself. The more stages and hosts a journey has, the more eggs the parasite makes. This is not waste. It is how a very fragile journey carries on, when most of it fails.
examples: If the chance at each of 4 stages is 1 in 10, about 10,000 eggs are needed for one adult.
A parasite with only 2 stages and the same odds needs about 100 eggs for one adult.
A louse lives on one head and does not need the chance of the outside world, so she lays only a few eggs a day.
explanations.art: A funnel with ten thousand dots at the wide top, one hundred in the middle after two gates, and a single dot at the narrow bottom after four gates.

explanations.concept: Filaria: a mosquito, the night and a swollen leg
explanations.context: This card follows the filaria worm, which is carried by mosquitoes. Many people in India live where it is found.
explanations.definition: Lymphatic filariasis is an illness caused by thread-like worms that live in the lymph vessels. It is spread by mosquito bites.
explanations.description: The commonest kind in India is spread by the Culex mosquito, who breeds in dirty, still water such as blocked drains. Adult worms live in the lymph vessels of a person for years. They make millions of tiny baby worms, which swim in the blood. Most of these baby worms are in the blood at night. This matches the night biting of the Culex mosquito. When the mosquito bites, she drinks some baby worms. In her body they grow for about two weeks, then move to her mouthparts. At her next bite they slip into the skin of a new person. Over many years the adult worms block lymph vessels, and a leg or another part of the body can swell. This is called elephantiasis. The swelling cannot be caught by touching a person. Care for the skin helps. In many districts of India, health workers offer everyone a yearly dose of tablets that clears the baby worms from the blood, so that the mosquitoes pick up none. After some years of this, the cycle stops. India has a large share of the world's cases, and works to eliminate them.
examples: A mosquito that bites a person at night is more likely to pick up the baby worms, because they are in the blood then.
Filling blocked drains and keeping water moving takes away the places where Culex breeds.
A yearly tablet for everyone stops the mosquitoes picking up baby worms, so the cycle cannot go on.
explanations.art: A cycle drawn as a loop: an adult worm in a lymph vessel, baby worms in blood at night, a mosquito biting, larvae growing in the mosquito, and larvae slipping into a new person's skin.

explanations.concept: Malaria in more depth: waves of fever, and a sleeping stage
explanations.context: This card goes deeper into the malaria parasite you met in Level 3. It explains why the fever comes in waves.
explanations.definition: The malaria parasite changes shape and place several times in her journey, and each stage has a different job.
explanations.description: A mosquito injects a stage called a sporozoite. She goes to the liver and multiplies there. Then many new parasites leave the liver and enter red blood cells. Inside each red cell they multiply again. After about two days, for the commonest kinds, many red cells burst at almost the same time and release a new crowd. The person shivers and then gets a high fever. This is why the fever returns every other day, in waves. A few days later it repeats, as the next crowd bursts out. Some of the parasites in the blood turn into a different stage that is made to be picked up by a mosquito. That is the way the parasite gets back to the insect. One kind, called vivax, has a special sleeping stage in the liver. It can wake weeks or months later and cause a relapse. So treatment must be complete, as the doctor says. India has several kinds of malaria, and people are tested by a quick blood test to find out which kind. In 2021 and 2023, the World Health Organization recommended the first two malaria vaccines, for children in places where malaria is common.
examples: Fever on Monday evening, again on Wednesday evening and again on Friday evening matches the two day wave of some kinds of malaria.
A person who felt well for months and then had malaria again may have had a relapse from a sleeping stage in the liver.
A blood test can find out which kind of malaria parasite a person has, and the doctor chooses the medicine from the kind.
explanations.art: A fever line that rises every second day like waves, with small pictures of red blood cells bursting under each peak.

explanations.concept: The liver fluke: three homes and a snail that makes copies
explanations.context: This card follows a parasite with three homes. It is common in cattle and buffalo in India.
explanations.definition: The liver fluke is a flat worm that lives in the liver of cattle and buffalo. Her life cycle needs a snail and a plant as well as the cow.
explanations.description: A fluke in a cow's liver lays eggs, which go out in the dung. If the dung falls in or near water, the egg hatches into a tiny swimmer. The swimmer finds a particular kind of pond snail and burrows into her. Inside the snail, one young fluke makes many copies of herself, each of which grows into a new swimming stage. The new stage leaves the snail, swims to a blade of grass or a water plant, and forms a tough cyst. A cow eats the plant. The cyst opens in her gut, and the young fluke travels to her liver and grows into an adult. People can also be infected if they eat raw water plants, though the usual host is the cow. Cooking water plants, and keeping dung out of ponds, break the journey. So does treating the herd with the medicine a vet gives. Cattle with liver flukes grow poorly and give less milk, so this parasite costs farmers a great deal.
examples: One snail that carries a young fluke can send out hundreds of new swimmers, which is how the odds are made up.
A cow that grazes at the edge of a pond can swallow cysts on the grass.
Cooking water plants kills the cysts, so raw water plants are the risk, and cooked ones are not.
explanations.art: A line of four pictures: a cow's dung falling by a pond, a snail with tiny swimmers coming out, a blade of grass with a tough cyst, and a cow eating the grass.

explanations.concept: Tapeworms: the hands and the food are links too
explanations.context: This card is about the tapeworm, and about how an illness can pass through eggs on hands and food.
explanations.definition: A tapeworm is a long flat worm that lives in the gut. The pork tapeworm can also cause a serious illness when her eggs are swallowed.
explanations.description: A tapeworm in the gut of a person makes segments full of eggs, which leave the body in the stool. If a pig eats the eggs, the young worms travel to the pig's muscle and form small cysts. A person who eats undercooked pork with cysts gets the adult tapeworm in the gut. That is the usual journey. But a person who carries the tapeworm can also pass eggs to others, on hands, in food and in water. If another person swallows these eggs, the young worms can travel to the muscles, the eyes or the brain. In the brain, they can cause fits. This is a common cause of fits in some parts of India. So even people who never eat pork can be infected, from the eggs on a food handler's hands or on vegetables. The links to break are the same ones you already know. Wash hands with soap after the toilet and before cooking. Wash vegetables well. Cook meat well. Use a toilet, so pigs cannot eat human stool. Treat people who carry the worm.
examples: A food handler who carries a tapeworm and does not wash after the toilet can spread eggs to the salad.
Cooking pork until it is no longer pink in the middle kills the cysts.
A toilet that keeps stool away from pigs and from water breaks the journey at the first link.
explanations.art: A loop: a person, stool on the ground, a pig, undercooked pork, and a person again, with a second dotted arrow from the stool to a plate of salad and to a hand.

explanations.concept: Mites and scabies: a short life cycle under the skin
explanations.context: This card is about a very small parasite that lives in the skin, and is more common than most people think.
explanations.definition: The scabies mite lives her whole life on one person, in tunnels in the top layer of the skin.
explanations.description: A female mite digs a shallow tunnel in the skin and lays a few eggs each day in it. The eggs hatch in a few days. The young mites grow up on the skin and mate, and the cycle begins again in about two weeks. A person usually passes the mites on by close skin contact, for example sleeping side by side, or holding hands for a long time. The itch comes from the body's reaction to the mites and what they leave behind. It usually begins a few weeks after the first infection, and is worst at night. The rash is often between the fingers, on the wrists, at the waist and on the feet. Scabies has nothing to do with dirt. It spreads easily where many people live close together. The treatment is a cream or lotion that a doctor or a pharmacist advises, put on the whole body. Everyone in the household, and anyone who has shared a bed, is treated on the same day. Clothes and bedding used in the past few days are washed hot, or kept in a sealed bag for a few days, because mites die away from a body after a short time.
examples: A whole family has to be treated on the same day, because a mite on one person can reach the others.
A pile of washed and sun-dried clothes carries no live mites, because mites die after a few days away from a body.
A child with scabies has done nothing wrong. Anyone can catch it from close contact.
explanations.art: A magnified drawing of a tunnel in the skin with a mite at one end and a trail of tiny eggs behind her.

explanations.concept: Resting stages: a cyst can wait in water
explanations.context: This card explains why some single-celled parasites can survive outside a body, and why boiling water matters.
explanations.definition: A cyst is a tough resting stage of a single-celled parasite, with a hard coat that protects it outside a body.
explanations.description: Amoeba and Giardia are single-celled parasites that live in the gut and cause loose motions. They live in a soft, active form in the gut. When they leave the body, many turn into cysts. A cyst has a hard coat, no feeding and no movement. It can wait in water or on food for days or weeks. When someone swallows it, the coat opens in the gut, and the parasite comes out and begins to feed. A cyst is tough. Some cysts of Giardia survive the amount of chlorine that is used to treat drinking water. So boiling the water, or passing it through a fine filter, is a better way to remove them. The cyst stage is why these parasites can travel in water over a long distance without a vector. It is also why washing hands and covering food matter.
examples: An amoeba is soft and active in the gut, and a cyst is hard and still in the water.
A cyst in a glass of water can wait for days until somebody drinks it.
A ceramic candle filter holds back cysts, because they are bigger than its tiny gaps.
explanations.art: Two drawings: a soft active amoeba in a gut, and a hard-coated cyst floating in a glass of water.

explanations.concept: How a parasite finds a host: breath, warmth and smell
explanations.context: This card says how parasites find a body in the first place. They sense the world and act on what they find.
explanations.definition: Parasites find hosts by sensing signs of a living body, such as warmth, breath, smell, light and movement.
explanations.description: A female mosquito follows the carbon dioxide in your breath from far away. When she is closer, she senses warmth and the smell of your skin. Scientists have found that the malaria mosquito, Anopheles, uses a heat-sensing receptor to find warm skin from a short distance. A tick waits on a blade of grass and senses breath and warmth from an animal passing by. Hookworm larvae in damp soil sense warmth and the touch of a bare foot. The tiny swimmers of a liver fluke are drawn to light and to the smell of a snail. A Guinea worm larva in the water cannot find a person, but a copepod swallows her. So each parasite uses the senses she has, and each reads the world in her own way. A mosquito reads breath and warmth as food. This is why a fan, which blows away breath and warmth, makes it harder for a mosquito to find you.
examples: A mosquito finds you more easily after you run, because you breathe out more carbon dioxide.
Hookworm larvae sense the touch of a bare foot, which is why chappals help.
A tick waits for hours on a blade of grass, ready to grip when the breath of an animal passes.
explanations.art: A mosquito flying towards a sleeping person with three dotted lines for breath, warmth and smell.

explanations.concept: Breaking a life cycle: find the weakest link
explanations.context: This card puts together how each journey in this unit can be broken, and why one cheap step can end an illness.
explanations.definition: A life cycle is only as hard to break as its weakest link. Breaking that one link ends the journey.
explanations.description: Every journey in this unit has a link that is cheap and easy to cut. Guinea worm: a cloth over the water pot, and keeping an infected foot out of the water. Filaria: filling blocked drains, mosquito nets, and a yearly tablet for everyone. Malaria: nets, covering water, and testing and treating every case. Liver fluke: keeping dung out of ponds, and cooking water plants. Tapeworm: soap after the toilet, washed vegetables, cooked meat, and a toilet. Scabies: treating the whole household on the same day. Notice that some of these protect one person, and others protect the whole village. A cloth over your own pot protects your own family. A yearly tablet for every person in a district protects everyone, because the cycle cannot start again. A good plan breaks the journey at more than one link, because a parasite that survives at one link can still be stopped at the next.
examples: In the Guinea worm campaign, filters and keeping feet out of the water were used together.
A yearly tablet for everyone in a district stops filaria from restarting, because no mosquito picks up baby worms.
Cooking water plants breaks the liver fluke's journey, while treating the herd breaks it at a second place.
explanations.art: A table of five journeys with a cut mark on the weakest link in each.

explanations.context: This card says how common parasites are among living beings, and how they came to be.
explanations.definition: A parasite is a being who lives on or in another and feeds from her. Scientists have found that this way of life began many separate times.
explanations.description: Parasitism is not rare or odd. By one count, many scientists think that a large share of all animal species are parasites at some point in their lives, though no one has counted them all. The ancestors of the tapeworm, the louse, the tick and the mosquito were free-living animals. They became parasites in different ways, many separate times, over millions of years. Free-living ancestors may have begun by eating the food or the waste of a larger animal and gradually stayed. Once inside, a parasite often loses parts she no longer needs, such as eyes or a gut. A tapeworm has no gut at all. She soaks up food through her skin from the food her host digests. A parasite's body is shaped by her journey as much as by her host. Each stage keeps what it needs and loses the rest.
examples: A tapeworm has no gut. She soaks up food from the food in her host's gut.
Mosquitoes, ticks and lice come from different ancestors, and all of them are parasites for part or all of their lives.
A louse has lost her wings, because she does not need them on a head.
explanations.art: A family tree of free-living animals with several different branches turning into parasites, each branch marked with a small louse, tick, tapeworm or mosquito.

explanations.concept: Should we try to wipe out a whole species of mosquito or parasite?
explanations.context: This card is about a real debate among scientists, with several views. It has no single right answer.
explanations.description: Mosquitoes carry malaria, filaria and dengue, and mosquito-borne illnesses kill very many people each year. New tools, such as gene drives, may one day let scientists spread a change through a whole mosquito species so that it dies out or cannot carry a parasite. Some scientists and doctors say it would save millions of lives. Others warn that nobody knows what we would lose, because mosquito larvae are food for fish, and adults are food for birds, bats and dragonflies. The Guinea worm raises a similar question. People worked hard to wipe it out, and almost have. Few argue for keeping it. But the question of whether to wipe out a whole kind of living being is bigger than medicine.
examples: A gene drive is a change in the genes that can spread through a whole population in only a few generations.
Of more than three thousand kinds of mosquito, only a small number bite people and carry illness.

perspectives.explanation: A few kinds of mosquito carry most of the illness, and wiping out those few kinds could save a great many lives, so we should try, carefully.
Mosquitoes are part of food webs. Taking away even one species could have effects that nobody can predict, so we should test small and go slowly.
The people who live where the mosquitoes are should decide, and they should be told the risks. A change that could spread across borders should not be made by one country or one company.

explanations.art: A mosquito in the centre of a food web, with arrows to fish, a bat and a dragonfly, and a question mark above her.

agreed.text: Many parasites need more than one host, and breaking the journey at one link can stop the whole cycle.
agreed.evidence: Guinea worm was stopped in India and in most of the world by cutting two links: filtering the water and keeping infected feet out of drinking water. No vaccine or cure was needed.

agreed.text: Guinea worm has been eliminated from India and is close to being wiped out from the world.
agreed.evidence: India was certified free of Guinea worm in 2000. From several million cases a year in the 1980s, the world fell to only a handful of human cases a year in recent years, according to the Carter Center and the World Health Organization.

agreed.text: Lymphatic filariasis is spread by mosquito bites, and giving a medicine to a whole community for several years can stop it.
agreed.evidence: In places where everyone at risk took the yearly tablets for several years, tests of the blood found far fewer baby worms, and mosquitoes picked up none. Many districts have stopped needing the tablets.

agreed.text: Malaria fever returns in waves because the parasites in the red blood cells burst out at about the same time.
agreed.evidence: Doctors have charted the fever of malaria patients for over a century, and the fevers repeat every 48 or 72 hours depending on the kind of parasite.

agreed.text: Parasites with several stages and hosts make very large numbers of eggs, because most of them are lost on the way.
agreed.evidence: Counts of eggs in the stool of infected people and animals show thousands of eggs a day, while only a tiny share of them find a new host.

agreed.text: A cloth filter holds back copepods but does not remove germs or chemicals from water.
agreed.evidence: Copepods are about a millimetre or more long, and the gaps in fine cotton are much smaller. Bacteria and viruses are hundreds or thousands of times smaller than the gaps, and pass through.

agreed.text: Scabies is caused by a mite that spreads by close skin contact, and treating the whole household on the same day stops it coming back.
agreed.evidence: Health agencies advise treating everyone in the household together because mites on one person can reach another before the cream has done its work.

challenging.claim: A parasite is a being who is only harmful, and the world would be better without them.
challenging.who: A common idea, and the view of many people who have suffered from parasites
challenging.for: Parasites cause great suffering. Malaria, filaria and worm infections harm millions of people, and most of them are poor.
challenging.against: Many ecologists point out that parasites are a very large share of living beings, and may help keep ecosystems steady. Wiping out an illness is a good aim. Wiping out a whole kind of living being is a bigger question.
challenging.context: This card is about whether parasites are only bad.

challenging.claim: You cannot get worm eggs if you are vegetarian, because worms come from meat.
challenging.for: The pork tapeworm does reach people through undercooked pork, and some worms are linked to meat.
challenging.against: Roundworm, threadworm and the eggs of the pork tapeworm can reach anyone through soil, unwashed vegetables, water and the hands of others. Washing hands and vegetables protects everyone, whatever they eat.
challenging.context: This card is about whether eating no meat keeps worms away.

challenging.claim: A cloth over the pot makes water safe to drink.
challenging.who: A common belief where cloth filters are used
challenging.for: A cloth does remove copepods that carry the Guinea worm, and the water looks clearer.
challenging.against: Germs, such as the bacteria of cholera or typhoid, and chemicals are much smaller than the gaps in a cloth, and pass through. A cloth stops the Guinea worm. For germs, the water must be boiled, treated or passed through a finer filter.
challenging.context: This card is about what a cloth filter can and cannot do.

challenging.for: The mosquitoes that carry malaria and filaria bite mostly from dusk to dawn.
challenging.against: The Aedes mosquito, which carries dengue, bites in the daytime and breeds in clean water in pots and trays. Protection is needed at all hours.
challenging.context: This card is about when mosquitoes bite.

challenging.claim: When the fever of malaria goes, the malaria has gone for good.
challenging.for: The fever stops soon after the medicine, and the person feels well.
challenging.against: One kind of malaria parasite has a sleeping stage in the liver that can wake weeks or months later and cause a relapse. A full course of treatment, as the doctor says, is needed to deal with it.
challenging.context: This card is about whether malaria is over when the fever ends.

challenging.claim: Scabies is caused by dirt, and only children who do not wash get it.
challenging.for: The rash and the scratching look untidy, and people link itching with dirt.
challenging.against: Scabies is caused by a mite that spreads by close skin contact. Anyone can get it, however clean, and it spreads easily where many people live close together.
challenging.context: This card is about a hurtful idea about scabies.

challenging.claim: A parasite that kills her host has done well.
challenging.for: A parasite that takes a lot from a host seems to be winning.
challenging.against: A parasite that kills her host too soon dies with the host, unless she has already passed on. Many parasites do best when the host lives long enough to spread them, which is why most parasites harm their host only a little.
challenging.context: This card is about whether it is good for a parasite to kill her host.

big_questions.q: A Guinea worm is a speck in a copepod, and then a worm as long as an arm in a person. Which one of those is the Guinea worm?
big_questions.hint: Think about size, shape and home at each stage, and what stays the same.

big_questions.q: A parasite lays thousands of eggs and almost all of them are lost. Is that waste, or is it how a fragile journey keeps going?
big_questions.hint: Think about the odds at each stage, multiplied together.

big_questions.q: A cloth catches a copepod but lets a germ pass. What decides whether a filter holds a thing back?
big_questions.hint: Think about the size of the gaps compared with the size of the thing.

big_questions.q: The malaria parasite changes her shape and her home several times. When does she stop being the same being?
big_questions.hint: Think about a caterpillar and a butterfly, and about yourself as a baby.

big_questions.q: Guinea worm is nearly gone, but kala-azar, filaria and many other parasites still harm millions of people in poor places. Why do some illnesses get attention sooner than others?
big_questions.hint: Think about who is ill, who pays for medicines, and who decides.

big_questions.q: A Guinea worm is a living being who is only going about her own life. Is it right to wipe out the very last one?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a farmer, a doctor and a Jain monk would each say.

big_questions.q: A female mosquito bites only to feed her eggs. Is she an enemy, or a mother finding food for her young?
big_questions.hint: Think about why she bites, and why that is also what makes her a danger.

big_questions.q: Whose water is a step well: the people's, the copepods', or the worms'? Who gets to decide what lives in it?
big_questions.hint: Think about everyone who depends on the same water, including the tiny animals.

big_questions.q: Nobody has ever seen a Guinea worm larva swim into a copepod without a lens. How can we know the parts of a journey that we cannot see?
big_questions.hint: Think about how Manson and Low found out, by cutting open mosquitoes, and what other tools help.

story.title: The Cloth on the Matka
story.note: The story is made up. The science and the history in it are true. The Guinea worm was spread by tiny water animals called copepods in step wells and ponds in dry parts of India. The worm takes about a year to grow in a person. Health workers taught people to filter water through cloth and to keep an infected foot out of drinking water. India was certified free of the worm in 2000.
text: Sunita lived in a village in Rajasthan, where the land is dry and every drop of water counts. In the middle of the village was a step well. Stone steps went down, and down, and down, until the last step touched green water.

Every morning, the women of the village climbed down with clay matkas, and climbed up again with the matkas full, balanced on their heads. Sunita went with her mother. She liked the cool air at the bottom, and the way her voice echoed.
But there was one thing Sunita did not like. That was the hot season before the rains, when the worm came.

Every year, a few people in the village woke up with a painful blister on a foot or a leg. This year it was Sunita's cousin Mohan. After a few days the blister burst, and a thin white thread showed at the top. "The worm," said Dadi, Sunita's grandmother. "It comes every year, like the heat."

Dadi showed Sunita what to do. Each day they wound a little more of the thread round a matchstick, slowly and gently, never pulling hard. If it broke, the foot would swell and hurt even more. It took many days. When the whole worm came out, she was as long as Sunita's arm.
Mohan's foot burned as if it was on fire. The only thing that eased it was cold water. So every afternoon he limped down the stone steps of the well and sat with his foot in the water, sighing.

One morning, a woman came to the village on a bicycle, with a cloth bag on the handlebar. She was Kamla Didi, the health worker. She sat under the neem tree and asked everyone, "Who has had the worm this year? Who had it before? Where do you get your water?" She wrote everything in a notebook.
Then she took a glass jar, filled it with water from Sunita's matka, and held it up to the sun. "Look closely," she said to Sunita. "Tell me what you see."
At first Sunita saw only clear water. Then she saw a speck, and then another. They were tiny white specks, no bigger than poppy seeds, and they were jerking about in the jar. "They move!" she said.

"They are tiny water animals," said Kamla Didi. "They live in every step well. They are harmless to look at. But some of them carry something much smaller inside." She tied a clean cotton cloth over the mouth of a second jar and poured the water through. The water ran into the jar. The white specks stayed on the cloth, small and wet.
Sunita stared. "The worm is in those?"

"Not the worm," said Kamla Didi. "A baby of the worm. You will have to work out the rest. I will give you three clues. One: only people who drink the well water get the worm. Two: nobody gets it from touching a sick person. Three: it comes out of the foot, and the foot goes into the water."

Sunita sat down in the dust. She took a stick and drew a foot. Then she drew the well. Then the white specks. Then a mouth drinking. Slowly she joined them with arrows. The arrows went round and came back to the foot. It was a circle.

"Mohan puts his foot in the well," she said. "The worm in his foot lets out her babies into the water. The white specks swallow them. Then Dadi drinks the water with the specks, and the baby worms grow inside her. A year later, she has a blister. And then she puts her foot in the well." She looked up. "It goes round and round. The worm never leaves the village."
"Good," said Kamla Didi. "Now, where can you cut a circle?"

Sunita looked at the circle for a long time. "Here," she said, and put the tip of her stick on the arrow between the well and the mouth. "A cloth on the matka. The specks stay on the cloth." Then she put the stick on the arrow between the foot and the well. "And here. Nobody puts a sore foot into the well."

Dadi laughed. "A girl of nine tells the whole village to keep their feet out of the well!" But Mohan, who was tired of limping, said, "I will soak my foot in a bucket at the top of the steps. And I will pour the water out on the dry ground, far from the well."
That evening, every woman in the village brought out an old soft cotton sari, washed it, folded it into layers and tied it over her matka.
Sunita did her part every morning. She poured the water through the cloth, and washed the cloth in the sun afterwards. She made sure nobody sat with a foot in the well.

But nothing changed at once. In the next hot season, a few people still woke up with blisters. Sunita's heart sank. "Wait," said Kamla Didi. "The worm takes a whole year to grow inside a person. Those people drank their water before we began. The cloth cannot help the water they have already drunk. We must wait one more year."

It was a long wait. A year later, in the hot months before the rains, Sunita climbed the steps and listened. Nobody limped. Mohan ran past her with a stick and a ball. There was no blister anywhere in the village.
Kamla Didi came back on her bicycle to count, and she was smiling. "Not one," she said. "You cut the circle in two places, Sunita. The worm could not find her way round."

Sunita looked down into the cool green water at the bottom of the well. Somewhere in it, the white specks were still swimming. They had done nothing wrong. They were only one stage in a long journey, and now the journey had a gap in it.
story.epiphany: A parasite's journey is a circle with links. The Guinea worm needs a foot in the water, and then the water in a mouth. Cutting one link, a cloth on the pot or a sore foot kept out of the well, stops the whole circle, even though nobody can see the worm.
ask: Which two links in the circle did Sunita cut, and how did she cut each?
Why did some people still get blisters in the first hot season after the cloths were used?
What did the cloth catch, and what would it not have caught?
Kamla Didi did not tell Sunita the answer. She gave clues. How did the clues help Sunita work it out?

roots.context: We have followed a worm through a person and a tiny water animal, and watched a cloth cut the circle. Now we ask what a journey through many bodies tells us about what a living being is.

deep_truth.truth: A Guinea worm begins as a speck in a tiny water animal. She ends as a worm as long as your arm, inside a person. Her shape, size and home all change, but she is one life from start to finish. A parasite is not one body but a journey through several bodies.
deep_truth.habit: We name a living being by the body we meet, such as a worm, a larva or a mosquito, and think she is that body. But a parasite is a speck, a young stage and an adult, each in a different body and a different home.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Sari Filter Test, the copepods that a cloth holds back are about a millimetre long. A Guinea worm larva inside one is about half a millimetre, and the adult female can be 80 centimetres, about 1,600 times longer. Cutting the journey at any one stage ends the whole life.

three.who_am_i: You were once a single cell, then a baby, then a child. Your shape, size and home have changed many times, and you still say you are the same person. A parasite's life makes the same question very plain.
three.what_is_life: Every being passes through many shapes and places in a life. A parasite shows it more clearly because her shapes and homes are so different from each other.
three.what_is_this_world: Water, copepods, people, snails and mosquitoes are joined into circles. A cloth over a pot can change the health of a whole village, because everything in the circle depends on every link.

roots.thread: The Guinea worm lives as a speck, a larva and a long worm, in water, in a copepod and in a person. No stage looks like the next, and none could live the whole life alone. What goes on is the journey itself, passed from body to body. Cut one link and the whole circle ends, however many stages it has. Your own life, from one cell to a grown person, is a thread of the same kind.

teachings.teaching: As the one who lives in this body passes through childhood, youth and old age, so the same one passes into another body. The wise are not troubled by this.
teachings.link: A Guinea worm passes through a speck, a larva and an adult, in water, in a copepod and in a person. The Gita points to the same idea: one life, many bodies in a row.

teachings.source: Heraclitus, as quoted by Plato in Cratylus 402a
teachings.teaching: Everything moves and nothing stays still, and you could not step twice into the same river.
teachings.link: The parasite is never the same twice, and yet she is the same life. Like the river, she is a flow and not a fixed thing.

science.text: A life cycle is a series of stages, each with its own body, size and home. In many parasites, the stages look nothing like each other.
Whether the stages of a life should be counted as one being or as several is a question about how we use words, and scientists have no single rule.

other_view.view: A being is one body, with one set of genes, in one place and time. A speck in a copepod and a worm in a person are different bodies, and in some parasites, like malaria, a single cell divides into thousands of new cells at each stage. They are a line of descent, not one being. Calling them one life is a way of speaking.

practice.title: The same hands
practice.say: Sit still. Think of a photograph of yourself as a baby. Now look at your hands. Nothing in them is the same as when you were a baby, and yet they are yours. Breathe in slowly and out slowly, three times. Then think of a Guinea worm as a speck, and as a long worm, and ask the same question.
practice.kid: Think of a photo of you as a baby. Look at your hands now. Breathe slowly three times. Are they the same?

ask: Which one is the Guinea worm: the speck in the copepod, the long worm in the foot, or the whole journey?
You have changed a great deal since you were a baby. What stays the same, and what makes you say you are the same person?
A cloth over a pot changed the health of a whole village. What other small changes in a circle can change a whole community?

games.title: Order the Journey: five life cycles to put right
games.context: This is a sorting game with cards. You get 25 mixed-up cards from five parasite journeys. You sort them into five journeys, put each in the right order, and then cut each journey at a weak link.

printables.title: 25 journey cards (the answer is on the back)

items.f: A person with a blister puts a foot into the pond. The worm lets out tiny larvae.
A copepod swallows the larvae. They grow inside her for about two weeks.
A person drinks water with the copepod in it. The larvae are freed in the gut.
The larvae grow, the worms mate, and the female grows for about a year.
The female moves to the skin of a foot and makes a painful blister.
Adult worms in a person's lymph vessels make baby worms that swim in the blood, mostly at night.
A Culex mosquito bites at night and drinks blood with baby worms in it.
In the mosquito, the baby worms grow for about two weeks and move to her mouthparts.
The mosquito bites a new person, and the larvae slip into the skin.
The larvae travel to the lymph vessels and grow into adults.
An Anopheles mosquito bites a person with malaria and drinks parasites with the blood.
The parasites grow in the mosquito and move to her saliva.
The mosquito bites a new person, and the parasites enter the blood and go to the liver.
The parasites multiply in the liver, then enter red blood cells and multiply again.
The red blood cells burst together, and the person shivers with fever.
A fluke in a cow's liver lays eggs, which leave the cow in the dung.
In water, an egg hatches into a tiny swimmer that finds a pond snail.
Inside the snail, the young fluke makes many copies of herself.
The new swimmers leave the snail and form tough cysts on grass or a water plant.
A cow eats the plant, and the young flukes travel to her liver.
A female mite digs a tunnel in a person's skin and lays eggs.
The eggs hatch in a few days.
The young mites grow up on the skin and mate.
A new female crawls on to another person during close skin contact.
The new female digs a tunnel, and the cycle begins again.

printables.title: 10 cut cards (the weak link it breaks is on the back)

items.f: CUT: a folded cloth over the water pot.
items.b: Guinea worm, between steps 2 and 3. The copepods are held back and cannot reach a mouth.

items.f: CUT: a person with a blister keeps the foot out of the pond.
items.b: Guinea worm, step 1. The larvae are never let out into the water.

items.f: CUT: a yearly tablet for everyone in the district.
items.b: Filaria, step 1. No baby worms are left in the blood for a mosquito to drink.

items.f: CUT: a mosquito net over the bed.
items.b: Filaria step 2, and malaria steps 1 and 3. The mosquito cannot bite the sleeper.

items.f: CUT: fill blocked drains and empty still water.
items.b: Filaria and malaria, before step 1. Fewer mosquitoes are born.

items.f: CUT: test and treat every case of malaria.
items.b: Malaria, step 1. A treated person has no parasites for a mosquito to drink.

items.f: CUT: keep dung out of the pond.
items.b: Liver fluke, between steps 1 and 2. The eggs never reach the water.

items.f: CUT: cook water plants before eating them.
items.b: Liver fluke, between steps 4 and 5. Heat kills the cysts.

items.f: CUT: treat the whole household on the same day.
items.b: Scabies mite, step 4. No mite is left to crawl on to another person.

items.f: CUT: wash clothes and bedding hot, or seal them away for a few days.
items.b: Scabies mite, step 4. Mites die away from a body after a short time.

rules: Shuffle the 25 journey cards and spread them with the writing side up. Do not turn them over yet.
Sort the cards into five journeys, with five cards in each. Then put each journey in order, from step 1 to step 5.
When you have finished, turn the cards over to check. The back says the journey and the step. Score 1 point for every journey that is in the right order.
With friends, play it as a race. The first player with all five journeys in the right order wins the sorting round. Playing alone? Use a clock, and try to beat your best time.
Then take the 10 cut cards. Read the front of one, and place it beside the link it breaks. Say why. Turn it over to check, and score 1 point for each correct one.
Add up the points. A tie is shared.

check.q: In the Guinea worm journey, why must a copepod come between the pond and the person?
options: The larvae must grow inside the copepod before they can infect a person
The copepod makes the pond water cold
The copepod brings the larvae in a bucket
check.why: The larvae that leave the foot are not yet ready to infect a person. They need about two weeks inside a copepod. That is why a cloth that holds back the copepods breaks the journey.

games.context: This is a guessing game. Each card gives three clues about a parasite, a carrier or a way of breaking a journey. The fewer clues you need, the more points you score.

items.b: A GUINEA WORM. The weak link is a cloth over the water pot.

items.f: 1. I am a single cell. 2. I burst out of red blood cells together. 3. Fever comes back in waves because of me.

rules: Shuffle the clue cards. One player is the reader. The reader holds a card, with the clues facing the other players and the answer hidden.

Then the reader reads the back of the card. Anyone who can say the weak link as well scores 1 more point.

A mosquito larva
A scabies mite

flow.say: Which weak links appeared more than once? Which one would protect the most people at the least cost?
flow.kid: Add up the points. Which weak link appeared most?

ask.q: Which weak link works against more than one parasite?
good: Washing hands with soap.
A mosquito net, or emptying still water.

setup.art: A child holding a card with the answer hidden while another child guesses, with a finger covering clues 2 and 3.
setup.caption: 1. The reader reads clue 1 only. Everyone guesses.

setup.art: A clue card turned over to show the answer and the weak link.
setup.caption: 2. Turn the card over and name the weak link.

experiments.title: The Sari Filter Test: how many layers of cloth does it take to catch a pretend copepod?
experiments.question: A cloth over the pot held back the tiny water animals that carried the Guinea worm. Which cloth, and how many layers of it, catches pretend copepods, and how much slower (in seconds) does the water flow when the cloth is finer?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which cloth, with how many layers, will catch all the pretend copepods? Which filter will let the water through the slowest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every test uses the same amount of water, the same number of seeds, the same glass and the same slow pour. Only the filter changes. You use 10 mustard seeds as big pretend copepods and 10 khus khus seeds as small ones. You time how long 100 millilitres of water takes to pass, and you count the seeds that get through into the glass. If the water takes more than 3 minutes, you stop timing and write more than 3 minutes.
results_table: Mustard seeds that got through (out of 10)
Khus khus seeds that got through (out of 10)

materials.item: about 70 mustard seeds and about 70 khus khus (poppy) seeds, as pretend big and small copepods. No khus khus? Use the finest rava and score it as none, a few or many.
a steel tea strainer
a square of thin, loose cloth about 25 centimetres wide, such as an old dupatta, muslin or gauze
a square of tightly woven old cotton about 25 centimetres wide, such as a worn sari, dhoti or bedsheet
2 clear glasses, which you use one at a time and dry between tests
a steel plate, to pour the water on and count the seeds
2 rubber bands, to hold the cloth over the glass
a small katori or cup that holds about 100 millilitres (use the same one every time; fill it once from a measuring jug to check), and a jug of tap water
a few drops of food colour or washable blue ink, or half a cup of strong leftover tea, and a sheet of white paper to hold behind the glass
a small plate to hold the six piles of seeds
a clock with a seconds hand, or a phone stopwatch

experiments.safety: Keep the seeds away from babies and small children, who may put them in their mouth or nose. Mustard and poppy seeds cause allergies in some people, so if anyone at home is allergic, use dry dal and rice grains instead, and wash hands after handling seeds. Nothing in this test is eaten or drunk, so do not taste the water. Food colour, ink and tea stain cloth and fingers, so use an old cloth, keep ink away from the mouth and eyes, and wash your hands afterwards. Wipe up spilt water so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Make the filters. Run six tests with seeds and one test with turmeric. Fill in the table and decide which filter is best.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar for each filter, as tall as the number of seeds that got through. Mark the filter that you would choose for a village pot.
experiments.context: In this experiment you pour water with pretend copepods through different cloths, and find which filter catches them, and what a finer filter costs in time.

setup.art: A clear glass with a square of loose cloth stretched over its mouth by a rubber band, sagging a little in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Stretch a cloth over a glass with a rubber band.

setup.art: A small katori of water with ten dark mustard seeds and ten pale khus khus seeds stirred in, being poured slowly on to the cloth.
setup.caption: 2. Stir 10 mustard and 10 khus khus seeds into 100 millilitres of water, and pour slowly.

setup.art: The water from the glass poured on to a steel plate, with a few seeds visible, and a child counting them.
setup.caption: 3. Pour the water that got through on to a plate and count the seeds.

setup.art: A clock beside the glass, with a timer, and the last drip of water falling through the cloth.
setup.caption: 4. Time how long it takes for the 100 millilitres to pass.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the cloths, the strainer and the seeds. 2. Say that the seeds stand in for copepods. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason. 4. Write the guesses at the top of the table.
flow.say: A copepod is about as big as a poppy seed. Mustard seeds are our big copepods, and khus khus are our small ones. Which filter will catch them all? Which will be the slowest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Seeds stand in for copepods. Which cloth will catch them all? Which will be slowest? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that filter will catch the seeds?
good: Its gaps are smaller than the seeds.
It is thicker, so there is less room to get through.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. A guess with a reason is a good start. If your child says the thicker cloth will be the slowest, ask why. One child with a parent: the parent pours and times, the child counts. Two to four children: share the jobs. One pours, one runs the clock, one counts seeds, one writes the table, and swap after each test. Everybody guesses first.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sari Filter Test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Count out 6 piles of 10 mustard seeds and 6 piles of 10 khus khus seeds on a plate. 2. Fold the loose cloth into 4 layers and keep another square as 1 layer. 3. Fold the tight cotton into 4 layers, another into 2, and keep another square as 1. 4. Write the name of each filter on the table.
flow.say: You need six piles of seeds, one for each test. Folding a cloth in half makes two layers. Folding it in half again makes four layers.
flow.kid: Count six piles of ten seeds of each kind. Fold the cloths into layers.

check.q: Why do we use exactly 10 seeds of each kind and 100 millilitres of water in every test?
options: So that the only difference between tests is the filter
So that the tests take longer
Because 10 is a lucky number
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If one test had more seeds or more water, we could not tell whether a different result came from the filter or from the amount.

flow.context: In this step you count the seeds and fold the cloths into layers.

flow.do: Test 1 and Test 2. 1. Put the steel strainer over a glass. 2. Stir one pile of each seed into 100 millilitres of water. 3. Pour slowly on the strainer and start the clock as you begin. 4. Stop the clock when the last drip falls. 5. Pour the water in the glass on to the steel plate and count the seeds. 6. Repeat with the loose cloth, 1 layer, held on a glass by a rubber band.
flow.say: Pour slowly, at the same speed each time. Start the clock as you begin to pour. Stop it at the last drip. Then count the seeds on the plate.
flow.kid: Pour the seeds and water through the strainer. Time it. Count the seeds that got through.
flow.parent: Let the cloth sag a little in the middle, like a shallow bowl. If water runs over the side of the glass, pour more slowly. Write 3 minutes or more if the water is still dripping after 3 minutes. The seeds left on the cloth can be rinsed off and set aside. Do not reuse them in the next pile.
flow.context: In this step you run Test 1 with the strainer and Test 2 with one layer of loose cloth.

flow.do: Test 3 and Test 4. 1. Put the loose cloth in 4 layers over a clean, dry glass. 2. Stir in a new pile of each seed, pour slowly, time it and count. 3. Do the same with the tight cotton in 1 layer. 4. Write both results.
flow.say: Same pour, same seeds, same time. Only the cloth is different. Write what you see.
flow.kid: Test the loose cloth in four layers. Then the tight cotton in one layer. Count and time.
flow.context: In this step you run Test 3 with four layers of loose cloth and Test 4 with one layer of tight cotton.
flow.parent: Wet cloth tends to sag. If the khus khus stick in the cloth and few reach the glass, rinse them off the cloth with a little water into a bowl rather than counting them as through.

flow.do: Test 5 and Test 6. 1. Put the tight cotton in 2 layers over a clean, dry glass. 2. Stir in a new pile of each seed, pour slowly, time it and count. 3. Do the same with the tight cotton in 4 layers. 4. Write both results.
flow.say: Now the tight cotton in two layers and in four layers. Do more layers catch more seeds? Do they make the water slower?
flow.kid: Test the tight cotton in two layers. Then in four layers. Count and time.
flow.parent: Four layers of tight cotton may take over 3 minutes. If so, write more than 3 minutes and move on. If every test catches every seed, try a looser cloth or the finest rava in place of khus khus. A time over 3 minutes is only written as more than 3 minutes. All times are your own: kitchen water, cloth and glass sizes change them, so compare the filters with each other, not with the made-up example. The seed counts in the example are also made up and typical, not promised.

check.q: A filter with more layers catches more seeds but lets the water through more slowly. Why does a finer filter flow more slowly?
options: The gaps are narrower and longer, so water has a harder path
The cloth is heavier
The seeds block the water
check.why: Water has to squeeze through the gaps. When there are more layers, the gaps are narrower and the path is longer, so less water passes each second. The weight of the cloth and the seeds are not the main reason.

flow.context: In this step you run Test 5 with two layers and Test 6 with four layers of tight cotton.

flow.do: Test 7, the colour test. 1. Stir a few drops of food colour or ink into 100 millilitres of water. 2. Pour it slowly through your finest cloth that passes 100 millilitres in under 3 minutes. 3. Hold the filtered water against white paper, beside the coloured water you started with. 4. Compare the colours.
flow.say: This water is coloured. We pour it through our finest usable filter. Is the water that comes out clear, or still coloured?
flow.kid: Stir colour into water. Pour it through your finest filter. Is the water still coloured?

ask.q: What does the yellow water tell us about what a cloth cannot catch?
good: Very tiny things, like the colour, pass through the gaps.
A cloth cannot catch germs, because they are much smaller than the gaps.

flow.parent: The water will come out almost as coloured as it went in, because dissolved colour is made of pieces far smaller than the gaps in any cloth. (Tea leaves, if you use tea, are caught, but the brown colour passes.) Germs are also far smaller than the gaps, so a cloth cannot catch them. This is why boiling is also needed. Do not use turmeric powder here: part of it is lumps, and the cloth catches those, so the result is unclear.
flow.context: In this step you test what the best cloth cannot catch.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: What do you think happened? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happened that way? Which filter would you choose for a village pot, and why?
flow.kid: Say what you think, what you saw, and why. Which filter would you choose?

ask.q: What I think, what I saw, and why?
good: What I think: a finer filter catches more but is slower. What I saw: four layers of tight cotton caught every seed and took longest. Why: the gaps are narrower.

ask.q: Which filter would you choose, and what did you trade away?
good: Two layers of tight cotton, which caught all the seeds in a short enough time.
The fastest filter that still catches every seed.

flow.context: In this step you say what you think, what you saw, and why.

flow.do: Pour the water down the sink and rinse the seeds off the cloths. Wash the cloths with soap and dry them. Wash your hands.
flow.say: Tidy up. In the Guinea worm story, a cloth like this saved a whole village. A cloth can hold back a copepod. It cannot hold back a germ.
flow.kid: Pour out the water. Wash the cloths. Wash your hands.
flow.think: A cloth holds back things bigger than its gaps. What else in our home works like a gate with gaps?
flow.context: In this step you clean up and think about filters.

experiments.title: Four Pots on the Balcony: where do mosquitoes lay their eggs?
experiments.question: A female mosquito lays her eggs on or near still water. If we put out four pots of water, each covered in a different way, in which pots will wrigglers grow?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which pots will have wrigglers after five days, and which will have none? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All four pots are the same size, hold the same amount of tap water, and stand side by side in the same shady place outside. Only the cover is different. Pot A has no cover. Pot B has a tight lid. Pot C has a fine net or thin cloth tied tight. Pot D has a few drops of cooking oil on the water. You count on the same day for all four.

materials.item: 4 pots or tubs of the same size, each holding about a litre, such as plastic tubs or steel vessels
tap water, about 750 millilitres for each pot. Leave the jug open for one day first, so the chlorine fades. Add 3 or 4 dry leaves to each pot.
a tight lid or a plate that covers one pot completely
a piece of fine net or thin cotton cloth, big enough to cover a pot, and a rubber band
cooking oil, a few drops
tape and a pen, to label the pots A, B, C and D
a white plate or tray, and a spoon, to count the wrigglers
a torch, and a magnifying glass if you have one
a shady place outside, such as a balcony, a window ledge or a terrace corner, away from the bedroom window

experiments.safety: This test grows mosquito wrigglers on purpose, so it runs for only five days. A grown-up empties and scrubs every pot on day 5, and on day 6 at the latest, before any wriggler can turn into a mosquito. Never leave the pots out for a week or while the family is away. Pour the water and wrigglers down the toilet and flush. Place the pots where they cannot tip over or fall from a balcony. Wash hands after the count. Bring the pots in if a sudden storm or strong wind is coming, and keep the oil away from the stove.

schedule.what: Set up the four pots in a shady place outside. Write your guesses.
Look at each pot with a torch. Draw what you see.
Count the wrigglers in each pot, then empty and scrub every pot.

experiments.record: Fill in the table on day 1, day 3 and day 5. Then draw a bar for each pot, as tall as the number of wrigglers you counted.
experiments.context: In this experiment you put out four pots of water covered in different ways, and find where mosquitoes lay their eggs. It shows how a life cycle can be broken before it begins.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: wrigglers counted on day 5

setup.art: Four identical pots in a row on a shaded balcony floor, labelled A, B, C and D, with A open, B with a plate over it, C with a net tied on, and D with a shiny film of oil.
setup.caption: 1. Set out four pots with the same water, each covered in a different way.

setup.art: A torch shining into an open pot of water, showing tiny dark wrigglers hanging from the surface like commas.
setup.caption: 2. On day 3, shine a torch into each pot and look at the surface.

setup.art: A white plate with a few wrigglers and a pupa curled in a little water, and a child counting with a spoon.
setup.caption: 3. On day 5, pour each pot into a white plate and count the wrigglers.

setup.art: A child pouring a pot of water into a toilet pan, with the empty pot upside down and a scrubbing brush on the floor.
setup.caption: 4. Empty and scrub every pot. Flush the water down the toilet.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the four pots and the covers. 2. Say that mosquitoes lay eggs on or near still water. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason. 4. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: A female mosquito needs still water for her eggs. We will put out four pots with four different covers. Which pots will have wrigglers? Which will have none? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four pots, four covers. Which will grow wrigglers? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think that pot will get wrigglers, or not?
good: The open pot lets mosquitoes in.
A lid stops mosquitoes landing on the water.
Oil makes it hard for wrigglers to breathe.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. In dry or cold weather no mosquitoes may come at all. If no pot grows wrigglers, that is still a result. Write it down and try again in a warmer or wetter week. Wrigglers usually show by day 3 to 5 in warm, damp weather, and most easily on a ground floor, a low balcony or near plants. On a high floor, or in cold, dry or very windy weather, nothing may come. Then say so honestly: the lid and net pots are still fair, but without a result in the open pot you cannot compare, so repeat in a warmer or wetter week. Counts in the example are made up, so your numbers will differ.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Four Pots test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Label four pots A, B, C and D with tape. 2. Pour the same amount of tap water into each. 3. Leave Pot A open. 4. Cover Pot B with a tight lid. 5. Tie a net or cloth tightly over Pot C. 6. Put a few drops of cooking oil on the water in Pot D. 7. Put the pots in a shady place outside. 8. Write the start day.
flow.say: The pots are the same. Only the covers are different. Put them side by side in the shade. Write today's date. We will look again on day 3 and day 5.
flow.kid: Label four pots. Pour the same water into each. Cover them in four ways.

check.q: Why are all four pots the same size, with the same water, in the same place?
options: So that the cover is the only thing that is different
So that the pots look tidy
Because mosquitoes prefer the same size
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If one pot were in the sun or held more water, we could not tell whether the cover or the place made the difference.

flow.context: In this step you set up the four pots on day 1.
flow.parent: One child with a parent: the child does the labels and pouring, the parent carries the pots outside. Two to four children: each child looks after one pot (labels, guess, day 3 drawing, day 5 count), and all four compare at the end.

flow.do: On day 3, look at each pot with a torch. Look at the surface and the walls just above the water. Draw what you see in each pot. Do not move the covers more than you need.
flow.say: Shine the torch across the water. Do you see tiny dark commas hanging from the surface? Those are wrigglers. Draw what you see in each pot.
flow.kid: Shine a torch into each pot. Look for tiny wrigglers. Draw what you see.
flow.parent: Wrigglers are tiny at first, about the size of a comma. They hang head-down from the surface and dive when the water is disturbed. A magnifying glass helps. A little rainwater or a stray leaf is not a problem. If you see a big wriggler with a fat head, that is a pupa, called a tumbler.
flow.context: In this step you look at the pots on day 3.

flow.do: On day 5, count the wrigglers in each pot. 1. Pour the water in one pot slowly on to a white plate. 2. Count the wrigglers that move. 3. Write the number in the table. 4. Do the same for the other pots. 5. Look for any pupae, which are tumblers.
flow.say: Pour slowly on to the white plate. The wrigglers show up dark against the plate. Count the ones that move. Do all four pots, one at a time.
flow.kid: Pour each pot slowly on to a white plate. Count the wrigglers. Write the number.
flow.parent: If a pot has too many wrigglers to count, write more than 20. Also mark the water line with tape on day 1 and on day 5, to see if any water was lost. If a lid stopped mosquitoes landing, the lid pot will be empty. If oil was put on the water, some wrigglers may be dead or struggling. Write what you see.

check.q: The covered pot with a tight lid had no wrigglers, and the open pot had many. What does this show?
options: A mosquito could not lay eggs on water she could not reach
Lids make the water too warm for wrigglers
Wrigglers do not like the dark
check.why: The only difference between the pots was the cover, so the lid kept the mosquito off the water. Wrigglers can only start where an egg has been laid. This is why covering water stores breaks the cycle at its first link.

flow.context: In this step you count the wrigglers on day 5.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table. 2. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: What do you think happened? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happened that way? Which cover would you use on a water drum?
flow.kid: Say what you think, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: What I think, what I saw, and why?
good: What I think: a cover stops mosquitoes laying eggs. What I saw: wrigglers only in the open pot. Why: the mosquito could not reach the water.

flow.context: In this step you say what you think, what you saw, and why.

flow.do: A grown-up pours the water from every pot down the toilet and flushes. Scrub each pot with a brush and soap and turn it upside down to dry. Wash your hands.
flow.say: Today we must empty every pot, so no wriggler can grow up into a mosquito. Why must we empty on day 5 or day 6 and not leave it for a week?
flow.kid: A grown-up pours out the water. Scrub the pots. Turn them upside down. Wash your hands.
flow.think: A wriggler needs about a week to become a mosquito. What would happen in a pot left out for two weeks?
flow.context: In this step you empty and scrub the pots.

activities.title: Wind a Worm: how long does a Guinea worm take to come out?

materials.item: 80 centimetres of thick thread, wool or string
a thin pencil or a flat ice-cream stick
a ruler and a pen

schedule.what: Measure 80 centimetres of string. Wind 2 centimetres on to a pencil. Work out how many days the whole worm would take.

activities.record: A small table of days for different lengths and speeds, a sentence saying how many days it would take to wind the whole worm, and a drawing of the string wound round the stick.
activities.context: In this activity you wind a pretend Guinea worm slowly on to a stick, the way it was done in villages, and work out how many days it takes.

setup.art: A length of thick string laid beside a forearm to show how long a Guinea worm can be.
setup.caption: 1. Cut 80 centimetres of string and lay it beside your arm.

setup.art: A short length of string wound neatly round a thin pencil, the rest hanging loose.
setup.caption: 2. Wind just 2 centimetres on to the stick. That is a day's work.

flow.do: 1. Cut an 80 centimetre piece of string. 2. Ask your child to guess how many days it would take to wind the whole string. Each day, only 2 centimetres are wound on. Write your guess.
flow.say: A Guinea worm can be as long as your arm, and it was drawn out a little each day. Today we pretend each day gives 2 centimetres. How many days do you think the whole worm would take? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A pretend worm, 80 centimetres long. Each day you may wind 2 centimetres. Guess how many days.
flow.context: This is the first step of Wind a Worm. You guess before you wind.
