flow.do: 1. Lay the string beside your arm. 2. Wind exactly 2 centimetres on to the stick, slowly and gently. 3. Stop. That is one day. 4. Measure what is left.
flow.say: Wind it slowly, never pull. Stop at 2 centimetres. That is a whole day's work. How much of the worm is still to come out?
flow.kid: Wind only 2 centimetres of string on to the stick. Slowly. Stop there.
flow.parent: In real life the worm was wound a little at a time, because if it broke, the rest would stay in the body and cause swelling and infection. A day's winding was usually a few centimetres.

check.q: Why was the worm wound out only a little at a time, and never pulled?
options: If it broke, the rest would stay in the body and cause pain and swelling
The stick could only hold a little
The worm was shy
check.why: A worm that breaks leaves her other half inside the body, where it can cause infection. Winding slowly lets the worm come out whole. The stick is not the reason.

flow.context: In this step you wind the first 2 centimetres of the worm.

flow.do: 1. Work out how many days the whole string would take. 2. Write the answer. 3. Try a 60 centimetre worm and a 100 centimetre worm, at 2 and at 3 centimetres a day. 4. Fill a small table. 5. Talk about the question below.
flow.say: 80 centimetres, 2 centimetres a day. How many days? Was your guess close? A Guinea worm larva is about half a millimetre long. How many times longer than the larva is the adult?
flow.kid: 80 divided by 2. How many days? Was your guess close?

ask.q: A larva is about half a millimetre. How many times longer is a worm of 80 centimetres?
good: 1,600 times longer. 80 centimetres is 800 millimetres, and 800 divided by one half is 1,600.

flow.think: One life, from a speck to an arm's length. Which one is the Guinea worm?
flow.context: In this step you work out the number of days and compare the sizes.
flow.parent: Real worms are about 60 to 100 centimetres long, and often take weeks to come out. Answers: 80 centimetres takes 40 days at 2 centimetres a day. 60 takes 30 or 20 days, 100 takes 50 or about 34 days. With two to four children, each child winds a worm of a different length and the group compares days. With one child, the parent picks the second length.

activities.title: Fever Chart Detective: which chart looks like malaria?

materials.item: a sheet of squared paper or plain paper, a pencil and a ruler
the three made-up charts of numbers in the steps below

schedule.what: Draw three fever charts from the numbers. Say which one is a wave, and say what you would do next.

activities.record: Three line graphs on one sheet, with a note on the one that has waves.
activities.context: In this activity you draw three made-up fever charts, and find the one with waves that matches the way malaria parasites burst out of red blood cells together.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: Patient B's fever at 6 in the evening

setup.art: Three small line graphs side by side on squared paper, one falling slowly, one rising and falling like waves, and one rising slowly.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a line graph for each patient.

setup.art: One graph circled, with two arrows pointing at the peaks two days apart.
setup.caption: 2. Circle the one with waves, and mark the peaks.

flow.do: 1. Draw three sets of axes with the days along the bottom and the temperature up the side. 2. Ask your child to guess what a malaria chart would look like.
flow.say: A malaria parasite bursts out of red blood cells all at the same time, about every two days. What shape do you think the fever chart will make? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw three graphs. Guess what a malaria chart looks like.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fever Chart Detective. You guess before you draw.
flow.parent: Alone: draw all three patients. In a group: one patient each, then swap and compare. Squared paper is not needed; mark a ruler line for each degree.

flow.do: Draw each patient's line. Patient A, evening readings from Monday to Friday: 38.5, 38.8, 38.2, 37.4, 36.8. Patient B, evening readings from Monday to Saturday: 39.8, 37.0, 39.9, 37.1, 40.0, 37.2. Patient C, evening readings from Monday to Friday: 37.8, 38.4, 38.9, 39.4, 39.8.
flow.say: Mark each reading with a dot. Join the dots with a line. Do it for all three patients. What shape does each make?
flow.kid: Draw a dot for each reading. Join the dots. Do all three patients.
flow.parent: These are made-up numbers. Patient A falls slowly, like many viral fevers. Patient B rises on every second evening, like waves, as in many kinds of malaria. Patient C climbs day by day, which doctors call a step-ladder, a pattern seen in typhoid. A pattern is a clue, and only a test can tell.

check.q: Patient B's fever peaks on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. If the pattern goes on, when is the next peak?
options: Sunday
Saturday
Tuesday
check.why: The peaks are two days apart: Monday, Wednesday, Friday. The next one is two days after Friday, which is Sunday. Saturday is a low day.

flow.context: In this step you draw the three fever charts.

flow.do: 1. Look at the three graphs together. 2. Ask which one has waves. 3. Ask why the waves happen.
flow.say: Which chart has waves? Why do you think a fever would go up and down in waves? What happens inside the blood every two days?
flow.kid: Which chart has waves? Why would the fever come in waves?

ask.q: Why does the fever of malaria come in waves?
good: The parasites burst out of the red blood cells at about the same time, every two days.
Each new crowd of parasites gives another fever.

ask.q: How many days apart are the peaks in Patient B, and what would Patient B temperature be on Sunday?
good: Two days apart. About 40 degrees, a peak, because the pattern repeats.

flow.think: Doctors use patterns as clues, but a blood test tells which parasite it is. Why is a test better than a pattern?
flow.context: In this step you find the chart with waves and ask why the waves happen.

activities.title: The Odds Gates: how many eggs does it take to make one adult?

materials.item: 40 beans, rice grains or small stones, as the eggs
a die from any board game. No die? Write 1 to 6 on six small papers, fold them, and draw one each time, putting it back.
a sheet of paper and a pencil, to write the table
4 small plates or cards, labelled Gate 1 to Gate 4

activities.safety: Keep the beans away from babies and small children, who may put them in their mouth or nose. If anyone has a food allergy, use stones or paper scraps.

schedule.what: Run 36 eggs through four gates with a die. Run it again with a snail that makes copies. Compare the two.

activities.record: A table with four rows, one for each gate, and the number of eggs that got in and got through, for both runs.
activities.context: In this activity you roll a die to send 36 pretend eggs through four gates of a parasite's journey, and see how few come out the other end.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: Gate 2: eaten by the right animal (roll 4 to 6)
Gate 3: reach a new host (roll 5 or 6)
Gate 4: grow into an adult (roll 4 to 6)

setup.art: Thirty-six beans in a heap on the left, four labelled plates in a row, and a single die in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Start with 36 beans, four gates and a die.

setup.art: A child rolling the die for one bean and moving it to the next plate, with a few beans left behind in a 'lost' heap.
setup.caption: 2. Roll for each bean at each gate. Beans that fail go in the lost heap.

flow.do: 1. Count out 36 beans. 2. Put the four plates in a row. 3. Ask your child to guess how many beans will get through all four gates.
flow.say: Each bean is an egg of a parasite. It must pass four gates to become an adult. Gate 1 is reaching water. Gate 2 is being eaten by the right animal. Gate 3 is reaching a new host. Gate 4 is growing up. How many of 36 will make it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: 36 eggs. Four gates. Guess how many get through. Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Odds Gates. You guess before you roll.

flow.do: 1. At Gate 1, roll the die once for each bean. A roll of 3, 4, 5 or 6 lets the bean through. A roll of 1 or 2 puts it in the lost heap. 2. At Gate 2, a roll of 4, 5 or 6 lets it through. 3. At Gate 3, a roll of 5 or 6. 4. At Gate 4, a roll of 4, 5 or 6. 5. Write the beans in and the beans through at each gate.
flow.say: Roll for every bean, one at a time. Each gate has its own rule. Write down how many beans go in and how many come out. How many reach the end?
flow.kid: Roll for each bean at each gate. Pass or lose. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: On average, about 24 beans pass Gate 1, about 12 pass Gate 2, about 4 pass Gate 3, and about 2 pass Gate 4. Dice give different numbers each time, and zero or three are both possible. That is chance at work. Rolling about 75 times takes time. With two to four children, split the beans: each child sends 9 or 12 beans through the gates, then add up all your counts. One child with a parent: take turns rolling. Run the plain run twice if you want to see how chance changes the answer.

check.q: Two thirds of the eggs pass Gate 1, half pass Gate 2, one third pass Gate 3, and half pass Gate 4. Why do so few reach the end?
options: Each gate removes a share, and the shares multiply
The die is unfair
Gate 4 is the hardest
check.why: Each gate loses some of the eggs that reach it, and what is left must pass the next gate. Two thirds of a half of a third of a half is one eighteenth. So only about 2 of 36 come out. No single gate is to blame.

flow.context: In this step you roll the die and send the eggs through the four gates.

flow.do: Now play the snail run. Put 36 beans through again. At Gate 3, every bean that passes is replaced by 3 beans. The young parasite makes copies of herself inside a snail. The 3 copies go on to Gate 4. Write the new table.
flow.say: Some parasites, like the liver fluke, make copies of themselves inside a snail. At Gate 3, each bean that passes becomes three beans. How many reach the end now?
flow.kid: Play again. At Gate 3, every bean that passes becomes three. How many reach the end now?
flow.parent: On average the snail run ends with about 6 beans instead of 2. Making copies in the middle of a journey makes up for the odds at the early gates. Roll for the bean stack at Gate 3 together to save time. If you run short on beans, use coins or paper scraps.
flow.context: In this step you run the gates again, with a snail that makes copies.

flow.do: Compare the two runs. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: How many came through in the plain run? How many in the snail run? Why can a parasite that lays thousands of eggs and one that makes copies in a snail both do well?
flow.kid: Compare the two runs. Which gave more adults? Why?

ask.q: Why does a parasite lay so many eggs?
good: Most of them are lost at one gate or another, so she needs a great many to get one through.
The chances at each gate multiply, so the odds at the end are small.

flow.think: If you could remove just one gate for a parasite, which one would you pick, and who would it help?
flow.context: In this step you compare the two runs.

activities.title: Make a Life-Cycle Wheel

materials.item: 2 paper plates, or 2 circles of thick card about 20 centimetres wide
scissors
a pin or a split pin, or a pencil and a lump of clay, to hold the two plates together
coloured pencils and a ruler

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the window in the top plate with scissors and pushes the pin through, because scissors and pins are sharp. Use a pencil pushed into a lump of clay for young children, so no pin point is exposed. Keep pins away from babies and small children.

schedule.what: Draw five stages of one parasite around a plate. Cut a window in the other plate. Join them and turn the wheel.

activities.record: The finished wheel, and a sentence saying which stages happen in which host.
activities.context: In this activity you make a turning wheel that shows the five stages of one parasite's journey, one at a time, through a window.

setup.art: A paper plate divided into five equal segments, each with a small drawing of one stage of the Guinea worm and a number.
setup.caption: 1. Divide a plate into five segments and draw one stage in each.

setup.art: A second plate with a wedge-shaped window cut out, pinned on top of the first, showing one stage through the window.
setup.caption: 2. Cut a window in the second plate, pin the two together and turn.

flow.do: 1. Choose one journey, such as the Guinea worm, filaria or malaria. 2. Look at the five steps of that journey in the cards. 3. Decide what to draw in each step.
flow.say: Pick a journey you like. Each plate segment shows one stage. Which five pictures will you draw?
flow.kid: Choose a journey. Decide what to draw for each of the five stages.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Life-Cycle Wheel. You choose a journey.

flow.do: 1. Divide one plate into five equal segments. 2. Draw one stage in each segment, in order, with a number. 3. Under each drawing, write the host it happens in: person, copepod, mosquito or snail.
flow.say: Draw the stages in order, round the plate. Write which host each stage is in.
flow.kid: Draw five stages round the plate. Write the number and the host under each.
flow.context: In this step you draw the five stages round the first plate.
flow.parent: Two to four children: each picks a different journey and makes a wheel, then swaps wheels to guess the stage in the window. One child with a parent: the parent plays the guesser. One more paper plate is cheap at a kirana or stationery shop. Thick card cut into circles works too.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts a wedge-shaped window in the second plate, as big as one segment. 2. Pin the second plate on top of the first at the centre. 3. Turn the top plate to show each stage in turn.
flow.say: The window shows one stage at a time. Turn it slowly. Say what happens at each stage, and which host it is in.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the window. Pin the plates. Turn the wheel.
flow.context: In this step you build the wheel and turn it.

flow.do: Show the wheel to someone at home and explain the journey. Then ask them which link they would cut.
flow.say: Explain your wheel to someone. Where would you cut the journey? Why there?
flow.kid: Show your wheel to someone. Explain the journey. Where would you cut it?

ask.q: Which stage is in a person, and which is in the carrier?
good: Answers depend on the journey chosen. For the Guinea worm, the adult is in a person and the young stage is in a copepod.

flow.context: In this step you explain your wheel to someone.

activities.title: Look at Our Own Water Filter

materials.item: the water filter, purifier, matka, tap or tank that your family uses for drinking water
a grown-up, who knows how it works and how it is cleaned
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up opens any filter or purifier. A child looks but does not touch electric parts. Do not drink water from a filter that has not been cleaned as the maker says.

schedule.what: Find out how your family cleans its drinking water. Write what each part of the filter holds back.

activities.record: A short note: the kind of filter, what it holds back, what it does not, and when it was last cleaned.
activities.context: In this activity you look at how your own family cleans its drinking water, and ask which links in a germ or parasite journey it cuts.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up looking at a wall-mounted water purifier with a label and a list of stages.
setup.caption: 1. Find your family's water filter and read how it works.

setup.art: A notebook page with four columns: filter part, what it holds back, what passes, and how it is cleaned.
setup.caption: 2. Write what each part holds back and what passes.

flow.do: 1. Find out how your family treats drinking water. It may be a ceramic candle filter, a UV purifier, an RO purifier, boiling, a cloth or none. 2. Ask your child to guess what it holds back.
flow.say: Our drinking water goes through something before we drink it. What do you think it holds back? Copepods, germs, or both? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: How does our family clean drinking water? Guess what it holds back.
flow.context: This is the first step of Look at Our Own Water Filter.

flow.do: 1. Read the label or the manual with a grown-up. 2. Write each part of the filter and what it does. 3. Use the guide in the parent note to check. 4. Time how long it takes to fill one glass. 5. Find out when it was last cleaned or changed.
flow.say: Read what each stage does. Which parts hold back big things like sand and copepods? Which parts deal with germs? Which does neither?
flow.kid: Read the label. Write what each part does.
flow.parent: A cloth or a mesh holds back large things such as copepods and grit. A ceramic candle has far smaller gaps and holds back many bacteria and cysts. A UV purifier damages the genes of germs, but needs clear water to work. An RO purifier forces water through a very fine membrane and removes many germs and dissolved salts. Boiling kills germs and parasites. None of these works well unless it is kept clean and the filter is changed on time. Siblings can each take one water source (kitchen tap, tank, matka, bottled can). No filter at home: look at a neighbour, a school or a shop, or read about one.

check.q: A family uses only a cloth over their pot. Which of these will it NOT remove?
options: Bacteria that cause typhoid
Copepods that carry Guinea worm
Grit from the tank
check.why: A cloth holds back things bigger than its gaps, such as copepods and grit. Bacteria are far smaller than the gaps, so they pass through. For bacteria the water must be boiled or treated.

flow.context: In this step you read how your filter works.

flow.do: Talk about whether the family's way of cleaning water breaks the journeys in this unit.
flow.say: Which journeys does our filter break? Which links does it leave open? Is there anything we could do to make it safer?
flow.kid: Which journeys does our filter break? Is there a gap?

ask.q: What could make our water safer?
good: Cleaning the filter on time.
Covering the storage vessel, using a ladle and not dipping hands.

flow.context: In this step you talk about the safety of your own water.

projects.title: A Comic of a Journey: tell a parasite's story in twelve panels

materials.item: 3 sheets of plain A4 paper, folded to make a small book, or chart paper
pencils, coloured pens and a ruler
a younger child, a grandparent or a neighbour to read the comic to

schedule.what: Choose one journey. Plan twelve panels in pencil. Mark the panel where you will cut the journey.
Draw and colour the final comic. Read it to someone and ask them where they would cut the journey.

projects.record: The finished comic, and one sentence about what the listener said.
projects.context: In this 2-day project you tell the story of one parasite in a twelve-panel comic, so that anyone can see where the journey can be cut.

setup.art: A sheet of paper divided into twelve equal boxes with a pencil sketch of a worm, a mosquito and a person in the first few boxes.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: divide a sheet into twelve panels and plan the story in pencil.

setup.art: A child reading a coloured comic to a younger child sitting beside her on a sofa, pointing at one panel.
setup.caption: 2. Day 2: draw the final comic and read it to someone.

flow.do: 1. Choose one journey from the unit, such as the Guinea worm, filaria, malaria or the liver fluke. 2. Divide the paper into twelve panels. 3. Plan the story in pencil, one stage in each panel or two. 4. Mark one panel with a scissors sign, where the journey is cut.
flow.say: A comic is a good way to show a journey. Which parasite will you pick? What will be in each panel? Which panel shows the cut?
flow.kid: Pick one journey. Plan twelve panels. Mark the panel where you cut it.

ask.q: Why does a comic help someone understand a life cycle?
good: It shows the stages in order, one at a time.
You can see where each stage happens, in which host.

flow.context: This is the first day of a 2-day project. You plan your comic.
flow.parent: One child with a parent: the parent helps with the plan and the listener question. Two to four children: each makes a comic of a different journey, or share one comic with 3 panels each. Use only pens and paper.

flow.do: 1. Draw and colour the twelve panels. 2. Write a few words in each. 3. Read the comic to someone. 4. Ask them where they would cut the journey, and why.
flow.say: Draw your comic neatly, with a few words in each panel. When you read it aloud, ask your listener where they would cut the journey. Do they choose the same place as you?
flow.kid: Draw and colour the comic. Read it to someone. Ask where they would cut it.
flow.wait: Day 2: draw the final comic and read it aloud.
flow.context: This is the second day of the project. You finish the comic and read it aloud.

challenges.title: The Village Pot Filter
challenges.problem: Design a filter for a clay pot or a bucket that holds back pretend copepods, lets one litre of water through in under five minutes, and can be washed and used again.
constraints: Use only things from home, such as old cotton cloth, a tea strainer, a net bag, string, rubber bands and a bowl.
The filter must hold back all 10 khus khus seeds and all 10 mustard seeds.
One litre of water must pass in under five minutes. If your tightest cloth is too slow, test a wider area, or use a longer limit such as ten minutes and say so.
A grown-up cuts any plastic bottle, and the edges are covered with tape.
materials: a thin loose cloth or net
a bowl or pot to pour into, and a jug
10 mustard seeds and 10 khus khus seeds for each test
a steel plate to pour the water on and count the seeds
challenges.safety: A grown-up cuts any plastic bottle and covers the sharp edges with tape. Keep the seeds away from babies and small children. Mustard and poppy seeds cause allergies in some people, so if anyone at home is allergic, use dry dal and rice grains instead. Wipe up spilt water so nobody slips, and wash the cloths and your hands afterwards.
general: Two layers of tight cotton tied over the mouth of the pot with string.
A tea strainer lined with one layer of tight cotton.
A cloth bag hung inside the mouth of the pot, so the water filters through the sides and base.
creative: A coarse net on top to hold back leaves and big grit, and a fine cloth below to catch the small copepods, so the fine cloth does not clog.
A cloth stretched over a wide ring, so that it has more area and the water passes more quickly.
A funnel made from a cut plastic bottle with a cloth in the neck, to pour from a jug without spilling.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your design. Build it and test it with seeds and one litre of water. Write how many seeds got through and how many seconds it took. Change one thing, such as the number of layers, and test again. Which design was best, and what did you trade away?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge that follows the Sari Filter Test. You build the best pot filter you can, and measure how well it works.

setup.art: A child sketching three pot-filter designs on paper: a cloth tied over a pot, a strainer lined with cloth and a hanging bag.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch some designs on paper.

setup.art: A filter tied over a clay pot, a litre of water being poured through it from a jug, with a clock beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Build the filter, pour one litre through, and time it.

setup.art: The water from the pot poured on to a steel plate to show any seeds that got through, with a child counting.
setup.caption: 3. Pour the water that got through on to a plate and count the seeds.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the constraints. Ask your child to sketch two or three designs.
flow.say: A village needs a filter that is cheap, fast and strong enough to hold back copepods. How could you build one? Draw your ideas first.
flow.kid: Draw two or three ideas for a pot filter.

ask.q: What makes a filter slow, and what makes it catch more?
good: More layers catch more and make it slower.
Smaller gaps catch more and let less water through.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Village Pot Filter challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Build your first design. Count out 10 mustard seeds and 10 khus khus seeds. Stir them into a litre of water. Pour the water slowly through the filter into the pot. Time how long it takes.
flow.say: Build your first filter. Pour one litre through, slowly. Start the clock as you begin and stop it at the last drip. How long did it take?
flow.kid: Build your filter. Pour a litre of water with seeds through it. Time it.
flow.parent: Tie the cloth tightly so that it does not slip into the pot. A funnel or a wide strainer holds a litre better than a cloth alone. If water is very slow, add a bigger area of cloth. Water flow depends on the area of cloth, so use the whole mouth of a pot or a steel vessel, not a small glass, or a litre will take much longer than five minutes. Pour in portions of 250 millilitres if the cloth overflows. Pour out all the filtered water on a plate to count the seeds; they sink to the bottom. One child with a parent: the child designs, the parent pours and times. Two to four children: each team builds one design and tests it, then compare.
flow.context: In this step you build your first design and test it.

flow.do: Pour the water in the pot on to a steel plate and count the seeds that got through. Write the number of seeds and the time.
flow.say: Pour the water on to a plate. How many seeds got through? Did the filter meet both rules, no seeds through and under five minutes?
flow.kid: Pour the water on a plate. Count the seeds. Did you meet both rules?

check.q: A filter catches every seed but takes ten minutes for a litre. What should the designer change?
options: Use fewer layers or a bigger area of cloth, and test again
Add more layers
Give up the idea of filtering
check.why: A filter must catch the seeds and also pass water fast enough. Fewer layers or a bigger area lets the water through faster. More layers would make it even slower.

flow.context: In this step you count the seeds that got through and check both rules.

flow.do: Talk about what to change, and test again if there is time.
flow.say: What would you change to get fewer seeds through or a faster flow? What did you trade away to get a better catch?
flow.kid: What would you change? What did you trade away?

challenges.title: The Foot-Soaking Station
challenges.problem: A person with a painful blister wants to cool a foot in water. Design a station near a village well where the person can soak a foot, so that none of the water from the foot flows back into the well.
constraints: Use a model made on a large tray with sand or soil, a small katori for the well and a small bowl for the station.
The station must be higher than the well, or the water must be able to run away from it.
Test with one cup of water coloured with turmeric. Measure the yellow water that reaches the well katori with a teaspoon or by the level: the goal is none.
The station must be easy for a person with a sore foot to use.
materials: a large tray or a baking dish
damp sand or garden soil (sand is not needed: soil from a plant pot works), to make slopes. Flour or rangoli powder is a fallback
a small katori sunk in the sand as the well
a small bowl as the station
a cup of water with half a teaspoon of turmeric stirred in
clay or foil to shape channels
general: Put the station on a slope that runs down away from the well.
Dig a channel from the station to a pit far from the well, so the water soaks into the ground.
Raise the well with a low wall, so water cannot run into it.
creative: A bucket on a raised platform, so the foot is cooled by pouring water over it and not by soaking.
A cloth-lined drain pit filled with gravel, where the foot water soaks away.
A station set up in a different part of the village, with a seat and a place to rest the leg.
challenges.your_turn: Build your model on the tray. Pour the cup of yellow water at the station. Watch where it goes. Change one thing, such as the slope or the channel, and test again. Which design kept the yellow water out of the well?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about one link in the Guinea worm's journey, the moment when larvae are let out into the water. You design a station that keeps them away from the well.

setup.art: A tray with sand shaped into a slope, a katori sunk into the low end as a well, and a small bowl at the top as a station.
setup.caption: 1. Build the village on a tray: a well, a station and a slope.

setup.art: A cup of yellow water being poured into the bowl at the station, the yellow trickling along a channel away from the well.
setup.caption: 2. Pour the yellow water at the station and watch where it flows.

flow.do: Talk about the problem. Ask your child to sketch two designs.
flow.say: A person with a blister wants cool water on her foot. But the worm lets out her young into any water that touches the blister. How can she cool her foot without the water ever reaching the well?
flow.kid: Draw two ideas for a foot-soaking station.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Foot-Soaking Station challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Build the model on the tray. Shape the sand into a slope, sink the katori for the well, and put the bowl for the station. Pour the cup of yellow water into the station bowl and watch where it flows.
flow.say: Build the village. Pour the yellow water at the station. Does any reach the well? Where does it go?
flow.kid: Build the model. Pour yellow water at the station. Watch where it goes.
flow.parent: Press the sand firmly so that water does not simply sink in. If all the yellow water sinks into the sand and none runs, that is also a result. Test a steeper slope. One child with a parent: the child builds, the parent pours the cup. Two to four children: each builds one design, then pour the same cup into each and compare how much yellow reaches the well. Sand that is very dry drinks up the water, so dampen it a little.
flow.context: In this step you build the model and test the first design.

flow.do: Change one thing, such as the slope or the channel. Pour a new cup of yellow water. Watch again.
flow.say: Change just one thing. Pour again. Did it help? Why?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Pour again. Does the yellow reach the well?

check.q: Water always runs downhill. Where should the used foot water go?
options: Along a slope or channel away from the well, to soak into the ground far from it
Along a channel that points at the well
Into a puddle right beside the well
check.why: Water follows the slope. Used foot water holds the young worms, so it must be led away from the well and soak into the ground far from it. A channel that points at the well, or a puddle beside it, would carry the young worms straight to the water people drink.

flow.context: In this step you change one thing and test again.

flow.do: Talk about what worked. Ask which link of the Guinea worm's journey your design cuts.
flow.say: Which design kept the yellow water out of the well? Which link of the journey did you cut? What would a village need to make it real?
flow.kid: Which design worked? Which link does it cut?

challenges.safety: Turmeric stains clothes, fingers and trays yellow, so use an old tray and wash your hands. Wipe up spilt water so nobody slips. Use a plastic or steel tray, not a good dish. Nothing in this model is drunk.

items.p: What is an intermediate host?
opts: A host where a young stage of a parasite grows, but where the parasite does not become an adult
The host where the parasite becomes an adult and lays eggs
A carrier that moves the parasite and does not get ill herself
items.why: The final host is where the adult lives and makes eggs, and a vector carries a parasite from one host to the next. An intermediate host is where a young stage grows.

items.p: Sort each stage by the host it lives in.
items: an adult Guinea worm under the skin of a foot
In a person
a young Guinea worm growing for two weeks
In a copepod
baby filaria worms growing and moving to the mouthparts
In a mosquito
a young liver fluke making hundreds of copies
In a snail
baby filaria worms swimming in the blood at night
In a person
malaria parasites growing in the stomach
In a mosquito
items.a: see items
items.why: A parasite spends different stages in different hosts. The adult Guinea worm and the baby filaria worms live in people, while their young stages grow in a copepod or a mosquito, and the young fluke multiplies in a snail.

items.p: You can catch the Guinea worm by touching a person who has one.
items.why: False. The Guinea worm is caught only by drinking water that holds a copepod with young worms inside.

items.p: A tiny water animal, about as big as a poppy seed, that carries the young Guinea worm is called a ________.
items.why: A copepod, sometimes called a water flea, is the Guinea worm's intermediate host.

items.p: Match each way of breaking a journey to the parasite it stops.
pairs: A folded cloth over the water pot
A yearly tablet for everyone in a district
Keeping dung out of ponds and cooking water plants
Treating the whole household on the same day
A mosquito net over the bed
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each journey has its own weak link. A cloth holds back copepods, a tablet clears baby worms from the blood, and a net stops the bite of a mosquito. Cooking and clean ponds stop the fluke, and treating the household stops mites.

items.p: Why does a finer filter let water through more slowly?
opts: The gaps are narrower and the path is longer, so less water passes each second
The cloth is heavier
The seeds block the water
items.why: Water has to squeeze through the gaps. Narrower gaps, and more layers, make it harder for water to pass, so the flow is slower.

items.p: Put the stages of a mosquito's life cycle in order.
items: Adult mosquito
Wriggler (larva)
Egg laid on or near still water
Tumbler (pupa)
a: Egg laid on or near still water
items.why: A mosquito starts as an egg, hatches into a wriggler that lives in water, turns into a tumbler, and then an adult flies out.

items.p: A cloth over a pot makes the water free of germs.
items.why: False. A cloth holds back things bigger than its gaps, such as copepods. Germs are far smaller than the gaps and pass through.

items.p: A village begins to filter its water this month. Why might new blisters still appear for another year?
items.a: A strong answer says that the Guinea worm takes about a year to grow inside a person. People who drank unfiltered water before the filters began may still show blisters, so the effect takes a year to show.
items.why: A long gap between cause and effect makes it hard to tell quickly whether a change has worked, which is why scientists wait and count.

items.p: Which of these is a vector?
opts: A mosquito that carries the malaria parasite from one person to another
The person who has malaria
The malaria parasite herself
items.why: A vector carries a parasite or a germ between hosts. The mosquito does this for malaria, while the person and the parasite are the host and the parasite.

items.p: The fever of malaria comes in waves because the parasites burst out of red blood cells at about the ________ time.
items.why: When many red cells burst together, a new crowd of parasites is released at once, and the body reacts with fever. The next burst brings the next wave.

items.p: Draw a circle of arrows that shows a parasite going from one host to a second host and back to the first. Mark one place where you would cut the circle.
items.a: A circle with two hosts, for example a person and a copepod or a mosquito, joined by arrows, with a scissors mark on one arrow.
items.why: A life cycle is a circle. Cutting it at any one link stops it from going round, which is why one cheap step can stop an illness.

items.p: Why does a parasite that must pass through several hosts lay so many eggs?
opts: Most are lost at one stage or another, so only a few make it
She wants to fill the host
More eggs make the host stronger
items.why: The odds at each stage multiply, so very few eggs finish the whole journey. A parasite with thousands of eggs gets a few adults.

items.p: Scabies is caused by dirt.
items.why: False. Scabies is caused by a mite that spreads by close skin contact. It can happen to anyone, however clean.

items.p: A town has many mosquitoes that carry malaria and filaria. Two health officers disagree about what to do.

views.says: Spend the money on nets, drains and tablets. They work now, and they save lives.
Nets and tablets are not enough. We must fix the drains and the water supply, so that there is no place for mosquitoes to breed.

items.ask: Who do you agree with, and why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer gives a reason, such as nets and tablets working quickly while fixing drains stops mosquitoes being born in the first place. It says what is right in the other view, and may suggest doing both.
items.why: The two plans cut different links. A good plan often cuts more than one link.

items.p: Name one way to break the journey of the filaria worm, and say which link it breaks.
items.a: For example: a yearly tablet for everyone in a district breaks the link where a mosquito picks up baby worms from the blood. A net breaks the bite. Emptying drains and still water breaks the link where mosquitoes are born.
items.why: A journey can be broken at several places, and each link has a different cost.

items.p: Which habit protects a family from tapeworm eggs?
opts: Washing hands with soap after the toilet and washing vegetables well
Eating only vegetables
Wearing chappals indoors
items.why: Eggs pass on hands, in food and in water, to anyone. Washing hands and vegetables protects everyone, whatever they eat.

items.p: A parasite's egg has a 1 in 10 chance of getting through each of 3 stages. About how many eggs are needed for one adult?
items.why: 10 times 10 times 10 is 1,000. The chances at each stage multiply, so the odds of finishing all three are 1 in 1,000.

items.p: A child pours seeds through a cloth. All the mustard seeds stay on the cloth, but some khus khus seeds get through. What does this tell you about the gaps in the cloth?
items.a: The gaps are bigger than a khus khus seed and smaller than a mustard seed. A filter lets through things smaller than its gaps and holds back things bigger than its gaps.
items.why: A filter is a size gate. Comparing which seeds pass and which do not gives the size of the gaps.

items.p: Two layers of tight cotton caught all the seeds and took 100 seconds for 100 millilitres. Four layers caught all the seeds and took more than 180 seconds. For a village that must filter a lot of water, which is the better choice?
opts: Two layers, because it protects just as well and is faster
Four layers, because more layers are always better
Neither, because cloth cannot filter
items.why: Both caught every seed, so the protection was the same. The two-layer filter was faster. More layers cost time and added no protection in this test.

items.p: The young Guinea worms swim from the water straight into a person's skin.
items.why: False. The larvae that leave the foot are not ready to infect a person. They must be swallowed by a copepod and grow in her for about two weeks first. People then swallow the copepod.

items.p: Is each one a final host, an intermediate host or a vector?
items: a person, for the Guinea worm
Final host
a copepod, for the Guinea worm
Intermediate host
a Culex mosquito, for the filaria worm
Vector
a pond snail, for the liver fluke
Intermediate host
a cow, for the liver fluke
Final host
an Anopheles mosquito, for the malaria parasite
Vector
items.a: see items
items.why: The final host holds the adult. An intermediate host holds a young stage that does not grow up there. A vector carries the parasite between hosts.

items.p: A mosquito who picks up filaria worms at night finds the baby worms in the person's ________.
items.why: The baby worms swim in the blood, mostly at night, which is when the Culex mosquito bites.

items.p: A person was treated for vivax malaria, felt well for months, and then had fever again. What is the most likely reason?
opts: A sleeping stage of the parasite in the liver woke up
The mosquito bit her through the net
The medicine had become a poison
items.why: Vivax malaria has a sleeping stage in the liver, which can wake weeks or months later and cause a relapse.

items.p: Why is it hard to prove that a cloth filter works against the Guinea worm in only one year?
items.a: The worm takes about a year to grow in a person, so people who drank unfiltered water before the filter began may still get blisters. You must wait, and compare with villages that did not use the filter.
items.why: When the effect comes long after the cause, scientists must wait and compare groups to find out what worked.

items.p: One child in a family has scabies. What best stops it spreading in the family?
opts: Treat the whole household on the same day
Wash only the sick child's hands
Wait to see whether anyone else itches
items.why: Mites can reach other people before their own itch starts, because the itch begins weeks after the first infection. Treating everyone together stops the mites going round again.

items.p: Scientists are developing a way to spread a change through a whole species of mosquito so that the mosquitoes cannot carry malaria.

views.who: Dr Meena, a doctor who treats malaria
views.says: Malaria kills very many children. If this is safe, we should use it as soon as we can.
Mosquitoes are part of food webs. We should test it small and slowly, and ask the people who live there.

items.ask: Which view do you find more convincing, and why? What evidence would help you decide?
items.a: A strong answer weighs the suffering that could be prevented against the risk of unknown effects. It names evidence that would help, such as small trials, what the species eats and what eats it, and what the local people want.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A good answer uses the evidence and says what it values.

items.p: Put the steps of the liver fluke's journey in order.
items: A cow eats the plant, and the young flukes travel to her liver
A fluke in a cow's liver lays eggs, which leave in the dung
The egg hatches in water and enters a pond snail
New swimmers leave the snail and form cysts on a water plant
a: A fluke in a cow's liver lays eggs, which leave in the dung
The egg hatches in water and enters a pond snail
New swimmers leave the snail and form cysts on a water plant
A cow eats the plant, and the young flukes travel to her liver
items.why: The journey goes from the cow to the dung, to the water and the snail, to a plant, and back to a cow.

items.p: A mosquito net protects a sleeper from malaria and filaria. Which link in the journey does it cut?
opts: The bite of the mosquito
The birth of the mosquito
The medicine of the sleeper
items.why: A net stops the mosquito reaching the skin, so no parasite is picked up and none is passed on.

items.p: A liver fluke makes hundreds of copies of herself inside a snail. How does that help the parasite, even though most eggs are lost?
items.a: It makes up for the odds. One egg that reaches a snail becomes hundreds of young flukes, so many more have a chance of reaching a cow.
items.why: A step that multiplies the parasite in the middle of the journey balances the steps that lose most of them.

items.p: A parasite that kills her host quickly is the most successful kind.
items.why: False. A parasite that kills her host too quickly dies with the host, unless she has already passed on. Many parasites do best when the host lives long enough to spread them.

items.p: Draw a circle of arrows showing how a person with a Guinea worm blister can infect other people through a village well. Then mark two places where you would cut it.
items.a: A circle of arrows: foot, water, copepod, mouth, person, with two marks, such as a cloth on the pot and a sore foot kept out of the well.
items.why: Cutting the circle in two places is safer, because a parasite that gets past one cut can still be stopped at the next.

items.p: How could scientists find out that filaria larvae develop inside mosquitoes?
opts: Let mosquitoes feed on a patient's blood, then cut some open at different times and look
Ask the mosquitoes
Look at a patient's foot
items.why: Looking inside the mosquito at different days shows the stages growing. That is how Manson found it, and how Low found them in the mouthparts.

items.p: The tough resting stage of a single-celled parasite, with a hard coat, is called a ________.
items.why: A cyst can wait in water for days and survives some chlorine, which is why boiling is better.

worksheets.title: Thinking About Parasites Like a Scientist (challenge)

items.p: A parasite's egg has a 1 in 5 chance at the first stage, 1 in 4 at the second and 1 in 10 at the third. About how many eggs are needed for one adult?
items.why: 5 times 4 is 20, and 20 times 10 is 200. The chances multiply, so about 200 eggs give one adult.

items.p: A head louse lives on one person for her whole life and lays only a few eggs a day. A liver fluke needs three hosts and lays very many. Explain the difference.
items.a: The louse has one host and almost no gates to pass. She is already at home, so her chance is high. The fluke has to pass a snail, a plant and a cow, so her chances multiply to a very small number, and she needs many eggs.
items.why: The number of eggs fits the length of the journey. More stages and hosts mean smaller odds, so more eggs.

items.p: Guinea worm has almost been wiped out, but malaria has not. Which fact makes the Guinea worm easier to wipe out?
opts: A person with the worm shows a visible blister, and the journey needs drinking water, so every case can be found and every pond treated
The Guinea worm is much more dangerous
Mosquitoes carry the Guinea worm
items.why: Every case shows itself as a blister, and the only way to catch the worm is to drink the water with copepods. That lets health workers find cases and cut the journey.

items.p: A country has money to do one thing. It can finish wiping out a rare parasite for good, or it can cut the cases of a very common one.

views.who: Dr Rekha, a public health doctor
views.says: Finish the rare one. Once it is gone, we never need to spend on it again.

views.who: Dr Sameera, a public health doctor
views.says: Reduce the common one. It harms many more people today, and every month we wait costs lives.

items.ask: Which plan do you find more convincing, and why? What would you want to know before deciding?
items.a: A strong answer weighs the people helped now against the long-term saving. It names things to find out, such as how many are ill, how close the rare parasite is to being gone, and the cost of each plan.
items.why: This is a question of fairness and of evidence. A good answer says what it values and what it would check.

items.p: A cloth filter stops the Guinea worm but not cholera. Explain this with the sizes of the things.
items.a: A copepod is about a millimetre or more, which is bigger than the gaps in a fine cloth, so the cloth stops it. The bacteria that cause cholera are hundreds of times smaller than the gaps, so they pass through.
items.why: A filter holds back things that are bigger than its gaps. What it lets through depends on size alone.

items.p: Parasites with several hosts always kill their hosts.
items.why: False. Most parasites harm their hosts only a little, because a parasite does best when the host lives long enough for her to spread.

items.p: Everyone at risk in a district takes filaria tablets each year. In the first year, a scientist finds baby worms in the blood of 120 of 1,000 people tested. After five years, she finds them in 3 of 1,000. What does this show?
opts: The programme is working, with about 40 times fewer people carrying baby worms
The programme has failed
The tablets made more worms
items.why: 120 divided by 3 is 40. The number of people carrying baby worms fell about 40 times, so fewer mosquitoes pick them up.

items.p: Does each step protect mainly your own family, or the whole community?
items: a cloth over your own water pot
Protects mainly your own family
a yearly tablet for everyone in a district
Protects the whole community
a net over your own bed
Protects mainly your own family
filling blocked drains in a town
Protects the whole community
a toilet for every home in a village
Protects the whole community
washing your own hands before eating
Protects mainly your own family
items.a: see items
items.why: Some steps protect the person who takes them. Steps that stop the parasite going round, like clearing it from a whole district, protect everyone, including people who never knew about it.

items.p: Draw a funnel that starts with 1,000 eggs. At each of four gates, half of the eggs are lost. Write the number of eggs left after every gate.
items.a: 1,000 at the top, then 500, 250, 125, and about 62 at the bottom.
items.why: Halving four times leaves 1,000 divided by 16, which is about 62. Each gate removes half of what reaches it.

items.p: In 1872 a doctor found baby worms in the blood of patients in Calcutta, but nobody knew how the worms got into the blood. Why does finding something in the blood not tell you how it got there?
items.a: A parasite in the blood could have come by many routes, such as the skin, the water or a bite. To find the route you must follow the parasite step by step, as Manson did by cutting open mosquitoes that had fed on a patient's blood.
items.why: Finding a parasite shows where it is, not how it arrived. A journey must be followed with tests.

items.p: A doctor guessed that people got filaria by drinking water with dead mosquitoes in it. Which finding showed that this was wrong?
opts: Grown young worms were found in the mosquito's mouthparts, ready to enter the skin at a bite
Mosquitoes were found near water
People were found with swollen legs
items.why: Young worms sitting in the mouthparts show that the bite is the route. Mosquitoes near water and swollen legs fit both ideas, so they could not decide between them.

items.p: The Culex mosquito who carries the filaria worm bites mostly at night, and the baby worms are mostly in the blood at night. Why does this match help the parasite?
items.a: The baby worms are in the blood when the mosquito is feeding, so she picks up many of them. If they were in the blood in the day, she would pick up few.
items.why: A parasite's timing is part of her journey. Being in the right place at the right time makes the cycle more likely to finish.

items.p: Giving everyone in a district at risk the same medicine on the same days is called mass drug ________.
items.why: Mass drug administration clears a parasite from the whole community, so the cycle cannot restart.

items.p: A liver fluke lives in the cows of a village. Why might treating the cows also protect the people?
opts: Fewer fluke eggs reach the ponds, so fewer snails and fewer plants carry the cysts
Cows breathe out the medicine
People eat the cows
items.why: Treated cows lay fewer eggs, so fewer snails are infected and fewer plants carry cysts. People who eat raw water plants then have less chance of meeting the fluke.

items.p: Choose one parasite journey from this unit. Which stage do you think is the hardest for the parasite to get through, and why?
items.a: Any journey with a reason. For example, for the Guinea worm, the hardest stage may be the larvae getting swallowed by a copepod, as the larvae must meet the right animal in a large pond. Answers should name a stage and give a reason about the odds.
items.why: Thinking about the hardest stage helps to find the weakest link, where a journey is easiest to cut.

quiz.p: In which host does a parasite become an adult and make eggs?
opts: The final host
The intermediate host
The vector
quiz.why: The final host holds the adult. An intermediate host holds a young stage, and a vector carries the parasite between hosts.

quiz.p: How does a person catch the Guinea worm?
opts: By drinking water with copepods that carry young worms
By touching a person with a blister
By a mosquito bite
quiz.why: The Guinea worm is caught only by swallowing a copepod that holds the young worms. Touching someone or a bite does not pass it on.

quiz.p: Two steps helped to stop the Guinea worm in villages. Which pair is right?
opts: Filtering drinking water through cloth, and keeping an infected foot out of the water
Wearing chappals, and washing vegetables
Sleeping under a net, and emptying drains
quiz.why: A cloth holds back the copepods that carry the young worms, and keeping an infected foot out of the water stops the larvae from being let out. Chappals and nets work against other parasites.

quiz.p: A cloth with fine gaps catches more than a cloth with wide gaps, but the water flows through more slowly. Why?
opts: Narrower gaps hold back more things but give water a harder path
Fine cloth is lighter
Fine cloth soaks up the water
quiz.why: A filter holds back everything bigger than its gaps. Narrower gaps catch more, and the water must squeeze through, so it is slower.

quiz.p: Which of these will a cloth over a pot NOT remove from water?
opts: Bacteria that cause typhoid
Copepods
Grit
quiz.why: A cloth holds back things bigger than its gaps. Bacteria are far smaller than the gaps and pass through, so the water must be boiled or treated for them.

quiz.p: If an egg has a 1 in 10 chance of getting through each of 4 stages, about how many eggs are needed to get one adult?
quiz.why: 10 times 10 times 10 times 10 is 10,000. The chances at each stage multiply.

quiz.p: Why does the fever of malaria come in waves?
opts: Parasites burst out of red blood cells at about the same time, again and again
The mosquito bites every second day
The medicine wears off every second day
quiz.why: Parasites multiply together inside red blood cells, and burst out at about the same time. Each burst brings a wave of fever.

quiz.p: Baby filaria worms are mostly in the blood at night. How does this help the parasite?
opts: It matches the time when the Culex mosquito bites, so she picks up many
It keeps the worms cool
It stops the person from feeling ill
quiz.why: A mosquito can only pick up the baby worms that are in the blood when she bites. Being in the blood at night means that more of them are picked up.

quiz.p: Which habit breaks the journey of tapeworm eggs from hands to mouths?
opts: Washing hands with soap after the toilet
Sleeping under a net
Wearing a hat
quiz.why: Tapeworm eggs can pass on hands and food. Soap after the toilet and before cooking cuts that link. A net and a hat do not.

quiz.p: Cooking water plants breaks the journey of which parasite?
opts: The liver fluke
The scabies mite
The head louse
quiz.why: The liver fluke forms tough cysts on water plants, which heat kills. Mites and lice live on bodies, not on plants.

quiz.p: A pot with a tight lid grows no wrigglers, and an open pot does. Which link of the mosquito's journey does the lid cut?
opts: The laying of eggs on or near the water
The growth of the adult
The bite of the mosquito
quiz.why: A female mosquito can only lay eggs on or near water she can reach. The lid cut the first link, so no wrigglers could start.

quiz.p: Why is treating only one person with scabies not enough?
opts: Other people at home may already have mites, and could pass them back
The cream only works on one person
Scabies cannot be treated
quiz.why: Mites spread by close contact, and the itch begins weeks later, so others may carry mites without knowing. Treating the whole household together stops the cycle.

quiz.p: In 1900, George Low found young worms in the mouthparts of mosquitoes. What did this show about how people catch filaria?
opts: The worms enter the skin when a mosquito bites
The worms come from drinking water
The worms come from the air
quiz.why: Young worms in the mouthparts are ready to slip into the skin at a bite. That showed that the earlier idea, that people drink the worms in water, was wrong.

applications: Health workers put cloth filters, larvicide and safe wells in villages to cut the Guinea worm's journey, and found and cared for every person with a blister.
On mass drug administration days, health workers in a district offer tablets to everyone at risk of filaria, so the cycle cannot restart.
In many cities, a weekly dry day asks every home to empty and scrub water containers, which cuts the mosquito's journey at the egg stage.
Health departments put small fish that eat mosquito larvae into ponds, wells and tanks, which cuts the journey at the wriggler stage.
Vets and farmers give cattle and buffalo medicine for liver flukes, and keep dung and ponds apart, to protect the animals and the milk.
Hospital labs look at a drop of blood under a microscope, or use a rapid test, to find which kind of malaria parasite a patient has.
Town water plants pass water through beds of sand before they add chlorine, so that large particles and copepods are held back first.
Meat inspectors and cooks make sure meat is cooked through, which cuts the journey of the pork tapeworm.
Scientists check whether mosquitoes in a district still die when they touch the insecticide on nets, because tough mosquitoes can take over, as in the Rice and Dal game.
Schools and anganwadis give deworming tablets to children twice a year, and teach hand-washing, to cut the journey of worm eggs from hands to mouths.

open_questions.q: Can the last Guinea worm cases be stopped, now that some dogs have been found with the worm?
open_questions.why_open: Since 2012, Guinea worms have been found in dogs in a few countries. Scientists think the dogs may catch them by eating fish or frogs that carry young worms, but they are still finding out.

open_questions.q: Will it be safe to use gene drives to change or remove whole species of mosquito?
open_questions.why_open: Gene drives are still being tested, and nobody knows all the effects on food webs. The decision involves science, ethics and the people who live where the mosquitoes are.

open_questions.q: Why are the baby filaria worms mostly in the blood at night, and what tells them when?
open_questions.why_open: The worms follow a daily clock that matches the biting time of the mosquito, but scientists have not fully worked out how the worms keep time.

open_questions.q: How does a sleeping malaria parasite in the liver know when to wake up?
open_questions.why_open: Some vivax parasites wake after weeks and some after months, and scientists still do not know what signals them.

open_questions.q: Is there a vaccine for every worm and fluke that infects people?
open_questions.why_open: There is no vaccine yet for most parasitic worms. They are large and complex, and their bodies are good at hiding from the body's defenders.

open_questions.q: Do parasites help to hold ecosystems steady?
open_questions.why_open: Parasites are a very large share of living beings, and some ecologists think they help to keep food webs balanced. Few studies have tested this, so the answer is not yet known.

jokes.a: She could not get a lift any other way.

jokes.j: What did the cloth say to the copepod?
Why was the mosquito such a good musician?
jokes.a: She always hit the high notes.

jokes.j: What did the snail say to the fluke?
jokes.a: You can copy yourself, but you cannot paste.

jokes.j: Why do parasites lay so many eggs?
jokes.a: The odds are against them, and they know their multiplication.

jokes.j: Why did the filaria worm only come out at night?

Why did the malaria parasite keep a diary?
jokes.a: She liked to keep her appointments every second day.

jokes.j: Why was the tea strainer a good detective?
jokes.a: It caught everything bigger than a clue.

maths.problem: In the Odds Gates, the chances at the four gates were two thirds, a half, a third and a half. Multiply them. What fraction of the eggs make it to the end? From 1,800 eggs, about how many become adults?
maths.answer: One eighteenth of the eggs. From 1,800 eggs, about 100 adults.
maths.explain: Two thirds times a half is two sixths, or one third. One third times one third is one ninth. One ninth times a half is one eighteenth. 1,800 divided by 18 is 100.
maths.context: In the Odds Gates, you roll a die to send 36 pretend eggs through four gates of a parasite's journey.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the chances at each gate shows how few eggs finish the whole journey, and why a parasite lays so many.

maths.problem: If an egg has a 1 in 10 chance at each of 4 stages, how many eggs are needed for one adult? If a worm lays 5,000 eggs a day, how many eggs does she lay in 30 days, and about how many adults will that make?
maths.answer: 10,000 eggs make one adult. In 30 days she lays 150,000 eggs, which makes about 15 adults.
maths.explain: 10 times 10 times 10 times 10 is 10,000. 5,000 times 30 is 150,000. 150,000 divided by 10,000 is 15. These are made-up numbers for practice.
maths.context: This is about why a parasite with several stages and hosts lays so many eggs.
maths.why_maths: Chaining the chances and then scaling up by the days shows how a very small chance can still keep a parasite going.

maths.problem: A pretend Guinea worm is 80 centimetres long. If 2 centimetres are wound out each day, how many days does it take? How many days if 3 centimetres are wound each day?
maths.answer: 40 days at 2 centimetres a day. About 27 days at 3 centimetres a day.
maths.explain: 80 divided by 2 is 40. 80 divided by 3 is 26 with 2 left over, so it takes 27 days, with the last day a short one.
maths.context: In Wind a Worm, you wind a pretend Guinea worm slowly on to a stick, a little each day.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the length by the amount wound each day shows why a worm that is wound out slowly takes weeks.

maths.problem: A Guinea worm larva is about half a millimetre long. The adult female is 80 centimetres long. How many times longer is the adult than the larva?
maths.explain: 80 centimetres is 800 millimetres. 800 divided by one half is the same as 800 times 2, which is 1,600.
maths.context: In Wind a Worm, you lay a pretend worm beside your arm to see how long a Guinea worm can grow.
maths.why_maths: Changing centimetres to millimetres lets you compare the two sizes directly and see how much one life changes.

maths.problem: In a made-up Sari Filter Test, 10 khus khus seeds were poured through each filter. The steel tea strainer let 9 through, the loose cloth with 1 layer let 7 through, the loose cloth with 4 layers let 1 through, and the tight cotton let none through. What percentage of the khus khus seeds did each filter catch?
maths.answer: The tea strainer caught 10 out of 100, the loose cloth with 1 layer caught 30 out of 100, the loose cloth with 4 layers caught 90 out of 100, and the tight cotton caught all 100 out of 100.
maths.explain: If 9 get through, 1 is caught, so 1 out of 10 is 10 percent. If 7 get through, 3 are caught, which is 30 percent. If 1 gets through, 9 are caught, which is 90 percent. If none get through, all 10 are caught, which is 100 percent.
maths.context: In the Sari Filter Test, you pour 10 khus khus seeds through each filter and count how many get through.
maths.why_maths: A percentage turns a count out of 10 into a share that is easy to compare, whatever the number of seeds.

chart.title: Made-up khus khus seeds that got through (out of 10)

maths.problem: In a test, 100 millilitres of water took 100 seconds to pass through two layers of tight cotton. How long would 1 litre take? How long would a pot of 20 litres take? Give both in minutes and hours as well as seconds.
maths.answer: 1 litre takes 1,000 seconds, about 16 minutes and 40 seconds. 20 litres take 20,000 seconds, about 5 hours and 33 minutes.
maths.explain: 1 litre is 10 lots of 100 millilitres, so 10 times 100 seconds is 1,000 seconds. 1,000 divided by 60 is 16 with 40 left over. 20 litres is 20 times 1,000, which is 20,000 seconds. 20,000 divided by 3,600 is 5 with 2,000 left, and 2,000 seconds is about 33 minutes.
maths.context: In the Sari Filter Test, you time how long 100 millilitres of water takes to pass through each filter.
maths.why_maths: Scaling a short test up to a pot shows that a very fine filter may be too slow for real use, which is why a design needs a large area.

maths.problem: A malaria patient has a fever peak on Monday evening, then every second day after that. On which days are the first six peaks? On which day is the sixth peak?
maths.answer: Monday, Wednesday, Friday, Sunday, Tuesday and Thursday. The sixth peak is on Thursday.
maths.explain: Count on two days each time. Monday, then Wednesday, Friday, Sunday, Tuesday and Thursday. The sixth is the one that falls on Thursday, ten days after the first.
maths.context: In the Fever Chart Detective, you draw a fever chart in which the fever peaks every second evening.
maths.why_maths: Continuing the pattern of the peaks predicts the next fever, which is how a doctor spots the rhythm of malaria.

maths.problem: In a made-up Four Pots test, Pot A had 34 wrigglers, Pot B had 0, Pot C had 0 and Pot D had 6. How many more wrigglers were in Pot A than in Pot D? What share of all the wrigglers were in Pot A?
maths.answer: 28 more. Pot A had 34 out of 40, which is 85 out of 100.
maths.explain: 34 minus 6 is 28. All together there were 34 plus 0 plus 0 plus 6, which is 40. 34 out of 40 is the same as 85 out of 100, because 34 divided by 40 is 0.85.
maths.context: In the Four Pots test, you count wrigglers in four pots covered in different ways.
maths.why_maths: Comparing counts, and the share in each pot, shows which cover did most to stop the mosquitoes.

maths.problem: A district has 2,400 people at risk of filaria. On tablet day, 85 out of every 100 people take the tablets. How many people take them, and how many miss them? Why might the people who miss them matter?
maths.answer: 2,040 people take them and 360 miss them. The people who miss them can still carry baby worms in the blood, and so can pass them to mosquitoes.
maths.explain: 2,400 divided by 100 is 24, and 24 times 85 is 2,040. 2,400 minus 2,040 is 360. The cycle can only stop if almost everyone takes the tablets.
maths.context: This is about mass drug administration, when everyone at risk in a district is offered the same tablets on the same days.
maths.why_maths: A percentage of a whole district tells how many people are left unprotected, who could keep the cycle going.

maths.problem: A person drinks water with Guinea worm larvae on 10 April. The blister usually shows 10 to 14 months later. Between which months of the following year would it appear? The larvae let out into water on 3 May need 14 days in a copepod. On which date are they ready to infect a person?
maths.answer: Between February and June of the following year. The larvae let out on 3 May are ready on 17 May.
maths.explain: 10 April plus 10 months is 10 February, a year later. 10 April plus 14 months is 10 June. 3 May plus 14 days is 17 May.
maths.context: This is about the long gap between drinking infected water and the blister, and about the two weeks the larvae spend in a copepod.
maths.why_maths: Counting months and days shows why it takes about a year to see whether a change to the water has worked.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1877, in Amoy in China, a Scottish doctor named Patrick Manson wondered how a tiny worm in people's blood, which could swell their legs, passed to new people. He let mosquitoes bite his gardener, who carried the worms, and later cut the mosquitoes open. He found the worms growing inside them. Nobody had shown before that an insect could carry a worm that infects people. But Manson made a wrong guess. He thought the mosquito died on the water, and that people got ill by drinking the water with the dead mosquito. For over twenty years, many doctors believed it. In 1900, another doctor, George Low, cut open mosquitoes and found the grown young worms in their mouthparts. They enter the skin when a mosquito bites. The drinking idea was wrong. Years before, in 1872, Timothy Lewis had found baby worms in the blood of patients in Calcutta.
how_we_found_out.who: Patrick Manson, George Low, and Timothy Lewis, with Manson's gardener whose blood held the worms
how_we_found_out.when: 1872 (baby worms found in Calcutta), 1877 (they grow in mosquitoes) and 1900 (they enter the skin by a bite)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Manson thought people caught the worm by drinking water in which infected mosquitoes had died. George Low showed that the young worms sit in the mosquito's mouthparts and enter the skin when she bites.
